  • Every release has: binaries, checksums, signatures, SBOM, third-party notices, release notes, known issues, and its support period (COMP).
  • Security fixes can ship as patch releases on supported versions.
  • The served model receives the same signed release; the control plane verifies the signature before rollout.

Cross-cutting concepts

Security

Sign-in and sessions

  • Passwords: Argon2id (OWASP parameters: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 lane), checked against a bundled list of breached passwords (a plain sorted list searched on this computer, so no network call is made; it is not a k-anonymity range file, M1-F48). A wrong password and an unknown e-mail get the same answer and the same timing.
  • Passkeys: WebAuthn (webauthn-rs), as a second step or on their own. Two-step codes: TOTP with backup codes (stored hashed).
  • Company sign-in: OIDC with PKCE; group claims map to Bugaboo groups.
  • Sessions: random 256-bit secrets, stored as a hash (SHA-256 with its own domain, so the hash of a session secret is never taken for one of an invitation); cookie __Host-bb_session (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax) that lives as long as a session may (the setting security.session-absolute-hours, default 24 hours). A session is pending after the password when the person has a second step (it can do nothing but finish it, for at most five minutes) and active after. A person who needs a second step and has none (the organization asks it of everybody with security.two-step-required, or any role they hold anywhere, through their own rows or a group's, has the switch of ADR-0025, decision 7) can only set one up: the question is asked at every request, so it counts from the next request, also in a session that was open before; every use case that is not part of setting up a code app or a passkey answers auth.second-step-required (403), GET /auth/me answers that the setup is required with no permission, and the next request after the code app is confirmed or the passkey is added is an ordinary one. Enforced by: the tests auth_03_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/second_step_by_role.rs and bb-store. A 401 for a session that has ended (the cookie belongs to no session, or it ran out) also makes the browser forget both cookies and what it cached (Clear-Site-Data: "cache", M2-F06); a session that is only waiting for its second step is not ended and is left alone. Enforced by: the tests m2_f06_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/session_ended.rs. A new secret is made at sign-in, when the second step is done, and when the password is changed (which also ends all other sessions), so a secret that was known earlier opens nothing. A session ends after the idle time (security.session-idle-minutes, default 30) or the absolute time; a session is marked as used at most once a minute; sessions nobody can use are removed inside every sign-in. Signing in from a browser that still has the cookie of an old session ends that old session, and a password alone shows nothing about the person (no name, address or administrator flag) until the second step is done. The two times are bounded settings (idle 5 minutes to 24 hours, absolute 1 hour to 30 days): a value outside is refused when it is stored and cut to the bounds when it is read. Where you're signed in lists the sessions (browser and system names, never the User-Agent text, and the shortened network) and ends any of them or all of them. The list holds at most 50 sessions and says when it was cut (truncated). Enforced by: the tests sec_12_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/sessions.rs (sign-out, list, end, end everywhere, idle and absolute timeouts, new secrets, password change, the old session of the browser), perf_02_the_list_of_sessions_has_a_cap_and_says_when_it_cut, sec_12_a_password_alone_shows_nothing_about_the_person_until_the_second_step_is_done, auth_01_the_session_times_have_bounds_and_values_are_cut_to_them in bb-core, and sec_12_only_sessions_nobody_can_use_are_purged in bb-store. The mark that a session was used (last_seen_at, at most once a minute) is made outside the request, one write at a time for a session, so a mark that is lost only makes the session stricter: the idle time counts from an older mark and the next request marks again.
  • How signing in is built: the mechanisms (passwords, tokens, CSRF token, TOTP, passkeys) are in bb-auth and do no I/O. The use cases are async fns in bb-app::auth; each takes the context Ctx (store, clock, hasher, passkeys, CSRF key, limit on failed tries, client network and browser) and an input type, depends on storage only through the port AuthStore (which is made of ports by job: accounts, sessions, the second step, invitations and access keys, next to the policy, project and settings ports; a read that is also needed inside a change is written once, queries!), and writes only through ChangeStore::record_change, so every change comes with its event and is undone together with it. A check inside a change (a code used twice, an invitation taken first) stops the change with AuthStore::aborted, which rolls back everything including the event. Adding a way to sign in (the code app, a passkey) asks for the password again, so a stolen session cannot add one. Waiting passkey challenges have a pool for each kind of ceremony (adding, second step, anonymous sign-in) and a cap for each network, so anonymous sign-in starts cannot keep the second step or an addition from starting. AuthApi lists the use cases once, with the store erased, so bb-api holds Arc<dyn AuthApi> and never names an adapter. bb-store implements the port (AuthStorage; tables from migration 2, every column with its personal-data mark), bb-api has the routes below /api/v1/auth (src/api/auth*.rs), and bb-server/src/wiring.rs builds it all at start. Enforced by: ARCH-DEPS, ARCH-EVENTS, ARCH-HTTP-EDGE, DATA-MARKS, and the flow tests in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/, which run every flow on both databases.
  • Setting up the first administrator (AUTH-09): at every start the server makes a new setup code when no administrator exists and prints it to the console only (never to the log file); only its hash is stored, and a new start replaces it. The code works once: it is used up in the same change that makes the administrator, setup is closed for good afterwards, and wrong codes count against the limit on failed tries. Enforced by: the tests auth_09_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/setup_and_password.rs.
  • The public address: the start-up setting public_url is the origin people type in the browser. Passkeys are tied to its host name; a server that listens on this computer only uses localhost and its port when the setting is missing, any other address needs the setting, a server behind trusted proxies needs it too (people reach it through the address of the proxy), and an address without a host name (an IP address) turns passkeys off. Enforced by: the tests auth_02_* in crates/bb-server/src/config.rs and auth_02_without_a_host_name_in_the_public_address_passkeys_are_off.
  • CSRF: three layers. (1) SameSite cookies. (2) An origin check, already in the API: every request below /api that is not GET, HEAD or OPTIONS must carry an Origin equal to the server's own origin or, when the browser sent no Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin. The own origin is the scheme plus the authority the browser asked for: the authority of the request address when there is one (HTTP/2 has no Host header), else Host; the scheme is https when the connection is TLS or when a trusted proxy says so (X-Forwarded-Proto, same trust rule as the client address: only from a listed proxy, only the last entry), else http; with neither the request is refused (fail closed) with the error request.wrong-origin (403, problem+json). Enforced by: the tests sec_06_* in crates/bb-api (cross-site, null, missing headers, same-origin, scheme, authority without Host) and the TLS + HTTP/2 test sec_06_over_tls_and_http2_the_origin_check_uses_the_authority_and_the_scheme. (3) A session-bound token: the value is derived on the server from the session (an HMAC of the session ID with a CSRF key), delivered in the page-readable cookie __Host-bb_csrf at sign-in and renewed with every new session ID; the server compares the x-csrf-token header with the value derived for the request's session in constant time, and refuses unsafe methods without a valid token with problem+json. The generated client reads the cookie and sends the header on every change. Layer 3 is the middleware csrf_check in crates/bb-api/src/api/auth.rs and covers every change below /api (a route added later is protected without anyone remembering): a change without a session cookie is answered with auth.not-signed-in (401), one with a session cookie and without the right token with request.wrong-token (403). Only the routes of people who have no session yet are left out: the routes that are public and change something in the route table permissions::ROUTES (setup, sign-in, sign-up, passkey sign-in, the invitation link; permissions::csrf_exempt reads them from the table, so there is no second list); they carry no secret a forged request could use and the origin check protects them. A request that comes with an access key (Authorization: Bearer bb_...) and no session cookie is left out of layers 2 and 3 as well: it has no cookie for a forged request to ride on, and a page of another website cannot send that header (there is no CORS; sec_06_a_page_of_another_website_cannot_send_a_key); with a session cookie a request is judged as a browser's, key or not. Enforced by: SEC-COOKIES (the cookie table) and the tests sec_12_a_change_needs_the_token_of_its_own_session, sec_12_every_route_that_changes_something_checks_the_token_except_signing_in_and_up (goes through every route of the API description) and sec_12_every_session_has_its_own_secret_and_its_own_csrf_token, and the TLS + HTTP/2 test sec_12_over_tls_and_http2_a_person_sets_up_signs_out_and_signs_in_again.
  • Cookies: only strictly necessary ones (the session and the CSRF token), so no consent banner is needed (COMP-13, PRIV-01). One module, crates/bb-api/src/cookies.rs, holds the table and is the only code that sets a cookie. Every name starts with __Host-, so browsers insist on Secure, Path=/ and no Domain; the module adds HttpOnly where script has no business reading the cookie. cargo xtask gen api writes the list "Cookies we use" to userDocs/cookies.md from the same table. Enforced by: SEC-COOKIES (reads the table; finds Set-Cookie, cookie libraries and document.cookie writes anywhere else).
  • Access keys (scripts, apps; AUTH-07): bb_ + a public prefix of 8 symbols + _ + a 256-bit secret in 52 symbols of the alphabet of codes (bb-auth, access_key.rs); only the hash of the secret is stored (SHA-256 in its own domain, found by the hash, so an unknown key and a wrong secret are the same lookup); the key is shown once, in an answer marked as a secret (never stored, never compressed). Making a key asks for the password again (a stolen session cannot make a key that outlives it); every key runs out (90 days unless the person picks another date, never later than the organization's longest time: the settings auth.access-key-default-days and auth.access-key-longest-days, at most 365; a key ends at a moment, so the form shows the region day of now plus the default, the latest day is the region day of now plus the longest time, a picked day is sent as the end of that day or the longest time from now if that comes first, and the server cuts a moment at most five minutes past the longest time to it and refuses a later one with request.invalid: expiry in access_keys.rs, expiry-day.ts in the form); the last use is kept to the minute. A script sends Authorization: Bearer bb_…; the use case takes the key where it takes a session (Ctx::actor), and the actor is the owner with the key's narrowing: at every request the owner's evaluation is narrowed by the key's choice and projects (Ctx::evaluation_of, which Ctx::require uses), so a key never holds more than its owner and follows the owner losing a role at once. An expired, a deleted, an unknown and a malformed key get the same answer (auth.not-signed-in); guessing is limited per network like failed passwords: the key is looked up first and only a lookup that fails reserves a try of the network (reserve_network), so a key that works never touches the counter and is never turned away by it, while a guess from a network over its limit is answered with 429. A key follows its owner's two-step requirement: while the owner is asked for a second step it is refused with auth.second-step-required (M2-F46). A key is judged before the body or the address of the request is read on the routes of the person's own sign-in data (require_session), so a key gets the same answer whatever it sent; the public prefix of a key as presented has to be the stored one, a clash of two public prefixes is retried once with a new secret, and a key that was used this minute writes nothing. A key that keeps See status reads GET /api/v1/admin/status (see_server_status, through the actor path; /auth/me stays session only). No key holds a permission of NOT_FOR_KEYS (Invite people, Manage people, Manage groups, Manage roles, Decide who has which role, Decide what roles see, Change organization settings, and since M3 and M4 Take over text someone else is editing (Edit anyway), Manage issue types, kinds of relation and layouts, Create, change and retire fields, Manage labels and tags and Manage workflows, since M6 See working hours of others and Change working hours of others, since M8 Enter work times for others, and since M9 Download someone's data and Remove people; seventeen in all, as in the list in the code): narrowing removes them whatever the choice, so inviting people, changing roles, changing the settings of the organization, taking over editing and changing how issues are described stay in the app (every use case that judges a permission goes through the actor, so the settings of WP-07 are covered as soon as they evaluate through it) (bb-policy, catalogue.rs, decision). Sign out everywhere deletes the person's keys (each one logged); a password change leaves them. No key reaches the owner's own sign-in data (password, second step, passkeys, sessions, keys): those use cases start at Ctx::active/Ctx::session, which turn a key away with auth.access-key-not-allowed and write it into the security log, so a route cannot forget it. A request that comes with a key and no session cookie needs no Origin and no CSRF token (there is no cookie for a forged request to ride on, and a page of another website cannot send the header: no CORS), is counted against the key as well as the network (access_key_requests_per_minute, default 300, per key), and its changes are recorded with the channel API. Making a key, deleting a key and a key that is turned away are in the security log (access_key.created, access_key.deleted, access_key.refused: the person and the key by ID; a refused key names nobody and shows the shortened network only, never the secret or the prefix). The routes of a person's own keys are /api/v1/access-keys (list, make, delete), /access-keys/rules (the default and the longest time, the single permissions with their topics) and /access-keys/project-choices (the projects the person may know, by short name, a page at a time); they declare own-account and take a session only. The form of My settings › Access keys (web/app/src/features/my-settings/access-keys) is made from them, and a person whose session must set up a second step is taken to the screen Set up your second step (features/sign-in). Enforced by: the tests auth_07_*, sec_14_* and sec_15_* in crates/bb-server/src/tests/sign_in/access_keys.rs and access_keys_http.rs, the Playwright tests auth_07_* and auth_03_* (web/app/e2e/access-keys.spec.ts, second-step-required.spec.ts, and the accessibility suite), the property test auth_07_a_key_can_do_only_what_its_owner_can_and_its_scopes_allow in bb-app, and SEC-SECRETS (the rule bugaboo-access-key of .gitleaks.toml).
  • MCP: an OAuth 2.1 authorization server inside Bugaboo, as ADR-0042 decides (decision 3: PKCE, which apps may register, the lifetimes and turnover of codes and tokens, hashes, scopes that only narrow like an access key; decision 4: the consent step, Connected apps with Take back, Sign out everywhere; decision 6: rate limits per grant and per person). An access key (Authorization: Bearer bb_…) is the other way in.

Browser protections

  • Content Security Policy: default-src 'self'; scripts and styles only from our own origin, no inline code, no eval (only 'wasm-unsafe-eval', which lets the browser start the WebAssembly module of the Markdown preview, ADR-0011); frame-ancestors 'none'; require-trusted-types-for 'script' with the one policy bugaboo-markdown, the only place that sets HTML from a string (SEC-RICHTEXT); images from our origin and data: only (outside images only if an admin allows the host).
  • Other headers: HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, COOP/CORP, a tight Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy: same-origin.
  • One header layer wraps the whole router, so pages, files, API answers, errors and 404s carry the same set. Enforced by: SEC-HEADERS (the check holds the one header table in headers.rs against the requirement: every required header is set, the policy lets no injected or foreign code run) and the integration tests, which read the table and assert the full set on a page, an asset, an API error and a 404.
  • HSTS is sent only when browsers reach us over HTTPS (here, or at a trusted proxy), and never with includeSubDomains (Bugaboo does not own the other names of its host). Lifetime: one day with a certificate Bugaboo made itself, so a person who trusts that certificate on localhost does not pin every other local tool to HTTPS; one year with a provided certificate or behind a trusted proxy. Enforced by: SEC-HEADERS (no includeSubDomains) and the tests sec_11_hsts_….
  • Compression (decision M2-Q2): Brotli or gzip, as the browser asks, for the text files of the app (from 256 bytes) and for JSON answers (application/json, application/problem+json) bigger than 1 KiB (JSON_COMPRESS_ABOVE_BYTES in bb-api router.rs, the one definition). Never for an answer that hands out a secret, whatever its size: a compressed answer that mixes a secret with text an attacker chooses can leak the secret (BREACH). The secret answers are the ones the cache rules mark (Performance, Cache rules in one place: a route the route table declares Secret, marked x-secret, or any answer that sets a cookie), and the compression skips every answer that carries that mark or a Set-Cookie header, so a route added later is covered by declaring its answer in the route table. Any other type that is not text (images, fonts, archives, other kinds of JSON) is left as it is. Enforced by: the tests sec_11_json_answers_are_compressed_above_1_kib_only, sec_11_json_answers_above_1_kib_are_compressed_and_smaller_ones_are_not, sec_11_an_answer_that_hands_out_a_secret_is_never_compressed_however_big, sec_11_files_keep_their_rules, perf_03_no_route_that_hands_out_a_secret_is_compressed (every route of the API description, with a big answer: the routes declared Secret are not compressed, all others are) and perf_03_a_big_answer_that_sets_a_cookie_is_never_compressed_whatever_the_route; review decides when a new content type needs the same care.
  • Slow and many clients: a client has 30 seconds (setting header_timeout_seconds) to send the headers of a request, which also ends idle keep-alive connections; HTTP/2 connections are pinged at the same interval. At most 1024 connections (setting max_connections) and 256 TLS handshakes run at once. Every API request has 30 seconds to finish, which also stops a request body that arrives too slowly (M1-F06). Enforced by: the tests sec_10_…slowly… and sec_10_no_more_connections….
  • Client address: the address of the connection is used, with IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:a.b.c.d) always treated as IPv4. X-Forwarded-For is believed only from a listed trusted proxy, and supports exactly one trusted hop: the last entry of the last header line is what the proxy itself saw; earlier entries are what the client claimed and are ignored. Enforced by: the tests sec_10_forwarded_for_… and sec_10_mapped_….
  • User content is rendered by one Markdown renderer with an allow list (ADR-0011). Attachments are downloaded, never rendered inline unless they are images or PDFs converted to safe previews.

Secrets and keys

  • A master key (outside the database) encrypts a key per secret (envelope encryption, XChaCha20-Poly1305). Secrets: mail password, AI keys, OIDC client secrets, webhook signing keys.
  • Where the keys live: keys/master.key (the master keys) and keys/log.key (the log key of the security log) in the data folder, which the server makes owner-only. master.key has one line per key, <id> <64 hex digits>, oldest first; the newest key wraps new secrets. log.key is one key that never changes, so a rotation does not touch the security log. The files are made on the first start only, replaced atomically (and the folder flushed) on a change, and on Unix refused when anybody but its owner can read them. Keys are read through and held in Zeroizing buffers and never show in Debug output. Enforced by: the key and secret tests of bb-store (SEC-16).
  • A missing key file is never replaced silently. The keys are made only when the database holds neither secrets nor a security log; otherwise Database::open_keys refuses with the catalogue message server.keys-missing ("Restore them from your backup"), because new keys could never read what the old ones protected. Enforced by: the test sec_16_missing_keys_stop_the_start_when_the_database_needs_them.
  • Stored form: each secret has its own random 256-bit key; the value is encrypted with it (24-byte random nonce), and that key is wrapped by the master key (own nonce). The ID of the master key is stored with the secret, and the secret's name (and the key ID) are authenticated data, so a row copied to another name or changed in any byte does not decrypt. Enforced by: the key and secret tests of bb-store.
  • Key rotation is a CLI command and an admin action (Database::rotate_master_key): add a key to the file, wrap every secret's key again with it in one transaction (values are not touched), and only then drop old keys that nothing uses. A stop half way leaves a state that still decrypts. Old keys decrypt, new keys encrypt. A running server follows a rotation made by the command line: the key ring looks at the modification time and size of master.key whenever it is asked for a key and reads the file again when it changed, so it never encrypts with a retired key; a write that was in flight while a key was retired is done again. Each secret is re-wrapped only if its row is still the one that was read (compare on the old wrapped key), so on PostgreSQL a secret replaced during the rotation is not overwritten with an old copy. Rotation is a rare administrator action; run it while no secret is being changed. Enforced by: the rotation tests of bb-store.
  • Backups hold no keys and are not encrypted in the MVP: whoever restores one elsewhere brings the keys with keys export and keys import, and a restore checks that the master key opens the backup's secrets first (ADR-0046). Encrypted backups are SEC-20 (V1). On Windows every key file has an access list of its own, set at every start and after a rotation (M1-F22).

Limits and abuse

  • Rate limits per IP and per account on sign-in, search, API and MCP; slow-down after failures, never a permanent lock that an attacker could trigger. Only failed tries are limited, and a try is counted before it is checked (M1-F27). A wrong password, a wrong code of the second step, a wrong password asked again before a sensitive change and a wrong setup code each reserve a slot of their account (the lower-case address, or the person after the password step) and of the client network when the try starts, and the slot counts as a failure from that moment, so many requests at the same time are not many guesses: no more than the allowance get through to be checked. A success gives the slot back (the account is cleared, the network gets its one try back), so signing in again and again never uses anything up. After the allowance (sign_in_failures_per_minute, default 10) a key waits for the rest of its window, also with the right password. Every window that ends with at least one failure makes the next one twice as long, up to 15 minutes, so pacing the tries just under the allowance does not help; a success (for the account) or a quiet time of 15 minutes ends the growth, and a key is never locked for good. The keys of a network are shared by many people and keep a window of a minute: they limit a flood and never grow. The wrong codes of the second step are counted under the key of the person, which only a finished second step clears; typing the password again before a sensitive change and confirming the code app have keys of their own, so a password that is right somewhere else does not reset the guesses at a code. A try that fails because the server failed (the database, the passkey library) gives its slot back, because it says nothing about the account; a request that was dropped stays counted. The sign-in cap and the failure keys use one size of network (IPv4 /24, IPv6 /48, the shortened address of the security log). Wrong codes of one half-finished sign-in are also counted without a window: after 10 the half-finished sign-in is ended and second_step.given_up is written to the security log, so whoever has the password starts again from the password. Wrong setup codes are counted per network, so nobody far away can lock the person at the console out. The counters are keyed hashes in memory; the failure that uses up an allowance is written to the security log once (sign_in.limited), so a flood does not fill the log. Enforced by: the tests sec_14_parallel_wrong_tries_at_one_account_get_no_more_than_the_allowance, sec_14_parallel_wrong_codes_at_one_half_finished_sign_in_get_no_more_than_the_allowance, sec_14_parallel_wrong_passwords_before_a_sensitive_change_get_no_more_than_the_allowance, sec_14_a_success_gives_the_try_back_also_when_tries_run_at_the_same_time, sec_14_only_failed_tries_count_and_a_success_clears_them, sec_14_ten_wrong_codes_end_the_half_finished_sign_in_and_are_written_down, auth_09_wrong_setup_codes_are_counted_per_network_not_for_everybody and sec_14_failures_of_one_network_are_limited_whatever_the_account in crates/bb-server/src/tests/, sec_14_only_a_finished_second_step_clears_the_wrong_codes_of_a_person, sec_14_a_failure_of_the_server_does_not_use_up_the_tries_of_a_person, sec_14_a_failure_of_the_server_does_not_use_up_the_tries_at_sign_in_and_before_a_change, sec_14_a_failure_of_the_server_does_not_use_up_the_tries_at_setup, and the tests sec_14_* in crates/bb-api/src/failures.rs (the growing wait also when paced, a network that does not grow, a full table) and sec_14_the_sign_in_cap_counts_per_network_in_the_size_the_failure_keys_use in crates/bb-api/src/limits.rs.
  • Rate limits (SEC-14) are counted per minute, in memory, per client network (an IPv4 address, an IPv6 /64; the canonical client address from above, never the raw header): all /api requests (setting rate_limit_per_minute, default 600) and sign-in attempts (setting sign_in_attempts_per_minute, default 60, a generous cap against floods) per client network (every try) and, as described above, failed tries (setting sign_in_failures_per_minute, default 10) per account, person and network, where the key is kept only as a keyed hash. Going over a limit answers 429 with Retry-After and the message error.rate-limit.exceeded; nothing is locked for longer than the minute. The limiter is Bugaboo's own fixed window instead of tower_governor: it needs no other dependency, reads the canonical client address that the logging layer works out, and gives sign-in the per-account hook that a one-key-per-layer limiter does not. When a table is full, expired counters go first (swept at most once per second, so a flood cannot make every request scan the table) and counters still running are never dropped; new clients then share one overflow counter in the general window, and are refused in the sign-in windows (fail closed). This is a trade-off accepted on purpose: while a table is full (100,000 clients within one minute), newcomers share one general bucket and new sign-in keys wait for the rest of the window; a per-network aggregate is M1-F35. Enforced by: review, backed by the tests sec_14_* in crates/bb-api (unit tests of the windows, integration tests for the 429 and for the client address).
  • Access keys have a limit of their own (SEC-14): a request that comes with a key counts against the key (the hash of what was presented, in memory, a window of a minute; access_key_requests_per_minute, default 300) besides the client network, so one script that runs wild uses up its own key and nobody else's; things that start like a key and are none share one counter, so they cannot use up the limit of a key that exists. Enforced by: the test sec_14_a_key_has_its_own_limit.
  • Search limits (SEC-17, M5-Q10): a search runs for at most 2 seconds (then search.too-slow, which asks to narrow it), has at most 50 filters (in (a, b) counts as many as it has values), within N steps at most 5, sort by at most 5 keys, a text of at most 4 096 bytes (ADR-0005, amendment M5), at most 10 different words in one contains (MAX_CONTAINS_WORDS, each word is another lookup in the text index), a word of contains that ends in * with at least 2 letters before it (MIN_PREFIX_CHARS, so one letter cannot match nearly every word; ADR-0016, amendment M5), a word of at most 255 bytes (MAX_WORD_BYTES: a longer one is refused by the checker, and the index does not keep one; ADR-0016, amendment M5), and pages of at most 100; each person may run 60 searches a minute (Quick search counts one search per pause in typing). The names that a suggestion offers (GET /api/v1/search/names) are small reads asked at nearly every key press, so they have an allowance of their own, 600 a minute per person (SUGGESTIONS_PER_MINUTE: about ten a second for a minute, far above what typing asks for and far below what a script does), counted apart from the searches so typing never uses up the allowance of searches; a name is at most 100 characters (NAME_MAX), an answer holds at most 20 names, and the store reads at most 5 pages of one name more than that (sec_17_suggestions_have_an_allowance_apart_from_searches). Every number is a named constant or a bounded setting in one place. Enforced by: the tests of M5 WP-02 and WP-04.
  • Request size limits; upload limits per project. API request bodies are limited to 1 MiB unless a route sets its own limit; a bigger body answers request.too-large. Enforced by: review, backed by the test sec_14_a_body_up_to_the_limit_is_read_and_a_bigger_one_is_refused_as_problem_json.

Authorization model

The decisions are ADR-0004 (one policy engine, Authorized<T>), ADR-0022 (Who sees people) and ADR-0025 (roles, groups and assignments on the project tree). This section is what bb-policy builds.

flowchart LR
  actor["Actor<br/>person · access key · AI app for a person ·<br/>agent (ADR-0029)"]
  groups["Groups"]
  assign["Who has which role<br/>person or group · role or No access ·<br/>whole organization, only this project,<br/>or this project and its sub-projects"]
  roles["Roles<br/>(permissions, field levels,<br/>Who sees people, two-step switch)"]
  fieldp["Field mask<br/>Hidden · Can see · Can change"]
  people["PersonRef<br/>name · role · Someone · Former user"]
  vis["Visibility groups<br/>restricted issues and documents (V1)"]
  scopes["Access key choice and projects<br/>(only narrow)"]
  actor --> groups --> assign
  actor --> assign
  assign --> roles --> fieldp
  roles --> people
  actor --> vis
  actor --> scopes

The permission catalogue

One enum, Permission in bb-policy. The four tables of this section and the next one that carry a GENERATED comment (the catalogue and, for the starting roles, their permissions, field levels and Who sees people levels) are written from that code by cargo xtask gen roles; DOC-GENERATED fails when one differs, so they are never edited by hand. The key is also the value of x-permission in the API description; the sentence is the message permission.<key>; the topic is the message permission-topic.<topic>. Counts says where a permission counts (ADR-0025, decision 1); Kind is what an access key's choice keeps (decision 8). Routes that need no single catalogue permission declare public, signed-in, own-account or by-record; the last is for the routes of edit locks and drafts, which work on any record by its kind and ID: what a person needs to change a record depends on its kind (for a project Change the project's name, short name and settings, for an issue Change issues), so the route lets in whoever is signed in, or comes with an access key, and the use case judges the record. A permission that no route asks for yet, because a use case judges it and its screen and routes come later, is named in tools/checks/permission-exemptions.toml with a reason that names the follow-up; the entry must go when a route asks for the permission. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS (every operation of the API description has x-permission with a key of the catalogue or one of the four words; every permission is asked by a route or named in the file; every permission and topic has its message).

  • A project permission given for the whole organization counts in every project; given on a project, in the project (and its sub-projects when the row says so).
  • The rows for the whole organization, and a role's own field and people levels, are changed only with Decide who has which role or Decide what roles see from a row for the whole organization.
  • Moving a project takes Move projects at the old and at the new parent; a project at the top level counts as inside the organization, so moving to or from the top takes the permission for the whole organization. Making a top-level project takes Create projects; a sub-project takes Create sub-projects at its parent. Renaming a project takes Change project settings; changing its short name takes that and also the right to create projects where the project sits (Create projects at the top level, Create sub-projects at the parent), because a short name that is taken is told only to people who may create projects there (decision: keep). A move shows its preview first (who gains or loses access or changes role, which fields and kinds of people information change for whom: the difference of two evaluations, bb_policy::preview_move) and is refused when somebody could take away a No access that applies to them after it and could not before (ADR-0025, decision 6; M2-F23). Changing a project's short name takes Change project settings and the right to create projects where the project sits, because only those people may be told that a short name is taken.
  • Later milestones add their permissions to the enum (issues M3, time M6, documents M11), each with its topic, sentence, kind and starting values. Enforced by: ARCH-PERMS (a permission without a route or a message fails).

Assignments

An assignment is one row of Who has which role:

PartValues
Whoa person, or a group
Whata role, or No access
Where it countsWhole organization (rows in Organization settings), Only this project, This project and its sub-projects (rows on a project); No access always covers This project and its sub-projects

A person or group can have several roles on one project, never a role and No access there. In the API the place is named applies_to with the values organization, project and project-and-sub-projects (glossary: Where it counts).

Evaluation

For an actor and a place (the organization, or a project and its parents), from one port call that loads the actor's groups and the rows of the place and its parents:

  1. Default deny: nobody signed in reaches only public routes; a signed-in person without an applicable row can do nothing and sees no project (SEC-01).
  2. Applicable rows: the actor's own rows and their groups' rows for the whole organization; rows on a parent project with This project and its sub-projects; rows on the project itself.
  3. Rank: the depth of the row's project (the whole organization lowest, a top-level project 1, its sub-projects 2, …), and at equal depth the person's own row above a group's row.
  4. No access: the highest-ranked No access row removes every role row of equal or lower rank. Roles from higher up, roles of the person's groups on the same project and other groups' roles on the same project are removed; a role given lower down, or to the person directly where a group has No access, stays. Decide who has which role from a removed row is kept when the row is strictly above the No access (a parent project or the whole organization), so nobody is locked out by a project below them; from a row at the depth of a No access that removes it, it is not (ADR-0025, decision 6).
  5. Permissions: the union of the remaining roles' permissions that count at this place (organization permissions only at the organization and only from rows for the whole organization).
  6. Narrowing: for an access key, keep only the permissions of the key's kinds (or the picked permissions), and nothing outside the key's projects and their sub-projects; a key with projects gets nothing for the whole organization.
  7. Field mask: for each field of the catalogue and each remaining role, the level set for that role on the nearest of the project and its parents, else the role's own level; the mask is the highest of these (Hidden < Can see < Can change), at most Can see for a See only key.
  8. Who sees people: for each kind, the level set for each remaining role the same way; the viewer's level is the most open (Names > Role only > Hidden).
  9. Visibility (restricted issues SEC-05, V1): an issue is visible if the actor sees its project and (it isn't restricted or the actor is in one of its visibility groups).

The evaluation is cached for the request and never longer (review: the cache lives in the request context; tests sec_03_a_role_taken_away_counts_from_the_next_request, auth_07_a_key_follows_its_owner_losing_a_role_at_once).

The field catalogue

Declared once in bb-core (fields): key, name (message issue-field.<key>), the thing it belongs to, and the kind of people information when it holds a person. Own fields join in M3 (CF-06) through one key type, FieldKey: either a built-in field of this catalogue or an own field (FieldKey::Own(FieldId)), so levels, masks, the field-permission page, history and fields= name both the same way and no list of own fields is written twice. A new own field starts Can see for every role that sees the project and Can change for Team member and above; whoever makes it can change that at once. Levels per issue type use the lookup of ADR-0027.

KeyNameBelongs toHolds a personKept from AI
