Database tests

Every repository test runs against SQLite and PostgreSQL (ADR-0003). Nothing is installed machine-wide (ADR-0024).

  • PostgreSQL 18.6 is a pinned tool in tools/dev/tools.toml. On Windows cargo xtask setup downloads the official binaries (checksum checked) into .tools/postgresql/. On Linux it uses the system PostgreSQL (on the PATH, or in the folder that pg_config --bindir names, as on GitHub's Ubuntu runners; no folder of the system is written down, and libpq-dev is the version of the installed server) and explains how to install it when missing.
  • cargo xtask db start | stop | reset | url manages a throwaway cluster in .tools/pg-data/. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, on the port postgres from tools/dev/ports.json (strict: a busy port is an error). Its random password lives in .tools/pg-password, never in the repository; on Windows the file is protected only by the inherited permissions of your user profile, on Unix it is readable by its owner only. All work folders share port 47240 (ADR-0023), so only one cargo xtask ci or db start runs at a time on a machine. db url prints the connection URL for tools of your own.
  • cargo xtask db run -- <command> starts the cluster if needed, runs the command with BB_TEST_DATABASES=sqlite,postgres, BB_TEST_POSTGRES_URL and BB_DB_PARITY_FILE set, stops the cluster again if it started it (also after an error), and then checks the parity record against ARCH-DB-PARITY and DATA-MIGRATIONS. Before the run it deletes the old record and any bbtest_* databases left behind by killed test programs; after a failure it deletes the record again, so an old or partial record never decides anything. cargo xtask ci runs the Rust tests this way, with cargo nextest run --workspace (the runner is pinned in tools/dev/tools.toml, its settings are in .config/nextest.toml): the tests of all test programs run side by side, one process for each test, so a test never relies on another one or on a shared static. The tests of the preview program start child programs with a time limit, so each takes every slot of the runner and runs alone; they run all the same. The runner does not run the examples in documentation comments, so the step Rust doc tests runs cargo test --workspace --doc. A single test by hand can still be run with cargo test.
  • Writing a test: bb_testing::each_database("name", async |db| { … }).await runs the body once per selected database. The body gets a typed pool (db.pool() is Pool::Sqlite or Pool::Postgres; tests/example_repository.rs in bb-testing shows the pattern). Each run gets an empty database of its own (a temporary file for SQLite, a freshly created and afterwards dropped database for PostgreSQL), so tests never see each other's data. Without BB_TEST_DATABASES, plain cargo test runs SQLite only.
  • The record target/db-parity.txt has one line per finished run (<database> <test name>). ARCH-DB-PARITY fails when a test ran on one database but not the other, or when a database did not run at all. DATA-MIGRATIONS additionally forbids .sql migration files and, once bb-store has migrations, wants its migrations test in the record for both databases. Both rules on the record run only inside cargo xtask db run, right after the tests; check all never reads a record left on disk (it can be from an older state of the code). There, ARCH-DB-PARITY checks that cargo xtask ci runs the Rust tests through db run, and DATA-MIGRATIONS checks for .sql files.

Enforced by: ARCH-DB-PARITY, DATA-MIGRATIONS.

Sample organization

A realistic, fully fictional organization used for development, end-to-end tests, demos and the optional "try it out" mode (OPS-12). Generated by cargo xtask dataset sample, deterministic from a seed (default 42), into SQLite or PostgreSQL. The people and the organization take a few seconds; the 10,000 issues with their comments take about six minutes (see Issues of the sample below), which is why --check and cargo xtask dev --sample make a smaller one.

Making it and using it

cargo xtask dataset sample [--seed N] [--database sqlite|postgres] [--issues N] [--out <folder>] [--check] runs the bb-sample program (crate bb-sample, architecture §4) as a process, so xtask does not link the store or the use cases. The program makes the organization through the same use cases the API calls: the first administrator with the setup code, everybody else as that administrator by invitation, so every change has its event and its security log entry and nothing is written to the database by hand. It is deterministic from the seed (default 42) with its own random source; it never reads the clock, because every date comes from one start moment that xtask passes in (now; a fixed moment for --check). The people and the organization take a few seconds on SQLite; the issues take minutes (see Issues of the sample).

  • Names: the folders the sample is made in, the names of its files and the environment variable of the PostgreSQL address are written once, in tools/dev/sample.json; xtask, the bb-sample program and the end-to-end tests all read that file.
  • What it makes in <out> (default target/sample, target/sample-postgres on PostgreSQL): data/ is a data folder that bugaboo serve --data-dir can start on (copy it first); sign-in.txt has one line per person (e-mail address, random password, role, name, the secret of the code app for the few people who have one, and the access key for the three who have one; the columns are separated by tabs, an empty column stays empty); dump.json is the canonical dump; sample.json marks the folder as made by the tool, so the next run may empty it and a folder with anything else in it is left alone. The passwords are random for every run and come from the operating system, never from the seed: no password is in the repository, and sign-in.txt is the only file that holds one (in target/, which Git ignores).
  • On PostgreSQL the program uses an empty database in the throwaway cluster of cargo xtask db (started and stopped by the command when needed). The address goes to the program in the environment variable BB_SAMPLE_DATABASE_URL, never on its command line.
  • People and organization: 50 fictional people with the mix of roles below, recorded in the plan (sample_people) and in the dump. After the people, bb_sample::Organization (the one filling of the extension point bb_sample::Later) makes the groups, the custom roles, the projects with their sub-projects and every row of Who has which role, as the first administrator, through the use cases of M2 (a change every second of the sample's clock, so the records come in the same order every time). Each person also chose a time zone and how dates and numbers are written, as they do in My settings, and a few have an access key. Names come from crates/bb-sample/data/names.toml, written for Bugaboo (no third-party name data); every address is under bugaboo.example. The people the demos name are the same whatever the seed: Ada Brandt (the administrator who runs the demo), Ana Moreno (a Contributor, on Website through the group External and nowhere else) and Ben Hale (a Team member for the whole organization, with No access on Android). The names of the groups, projects and custom roles are written once, in tools/dev/sample.json, which the program, xtask and the end-to-end tests read.
  • Issues of the sample (M3 WP-11): after the organization, bb_sample::Everything (the filling of the extension point that bb-sample runs) makes the issues of Projects below: the starting issue types and kinds of relation, how each project gives out its IDs, the own fields Severity, Platforms and Customer, the groups of labels and the labels, then every issue, sub-issue, tag, label, status change, relation and comment (some edited), and at the end one edit lock held and one draft waiting. All of it goes through the use cases, one change at a time, by the Administrators and Team members of the whole organization, each signed in on the working days they work (Monday to Friday, from nine, the clock of the sample running through eighteen months), so every date is a working day and every issue has a person who made it. The plan (crates/bb-sample/src/issues_plan.rs) has no database in it: it is worked out from the seed and the counts of tools/dev/sample.json (issues: the full count, the small count, the share of each type, of each project and place, the own fields, labels and tags, the numbers of relations and comments), and its words are in crates/bb-sample/data/issues.toml. --issues N scales every count to N issues (the full sample is issues.total, 10,000; --check and cargo xtask dev --sample make issues.smallTotal, 500). The readable IDs of the projects with Random IDs are the only thing that differs from run to run, and the dump leaves them out. No issue is restricted, and there are no releases. The history of every issue is read from the events at the end (what the daily job history.catch-up does), so the first page that shows one does not have to. The program is built with optimisations for this, as it runs about seventy thousand use cases: the full sample takes about six minutes on SQLite (the people and the organization, three seconds), the small one twenty seconds. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the dump of every --check run holds the numbers of the plan).
  • Using it in browser tests: cargo xtask dev --sample makes a fresh sample and starts the server on it (it prints where sign-in.txt is). A file of end-to-end tests that says test.use({ sample: true }) gets a server on a fresh copy of target/sample/data (one server per Playwright worker, ADR-0023 ports) and reads the people from samplePeople() (web/app/e2e/support/sample.ts). cargo xtask ci makes the sample in the background, beside the Rust tests and the steps up to the browser tests, which wait for it (its output is in target/step-create-the-sample-organization.log and is shown where they wait; a failure fails the run); by hand, run cargo xtask dataset sample first. The M1 tests of setup and signing in still start from an empty data folder.
  • Working together (M4 WP-10): the same program goes on after the issues, in three parts, all through the use cases. (1) Before the issues the project OPS gets a workflow of its own, Operations, made the way the editor makes it (Create, the edit lock, Publish): the starting workflow with the status change Open to In progress asking for Assigned to (Ask for); every other place keeps the starter workflows Simple, Bug and Development of the first start. The walk of the status changes (Maker::status) supplies what a change asks for. (2) After the issues Maker::work_together (together.rs, together_files.rs) lets the people who are not on the team do their part (M3-F111): the Viewers follow issues (viewerFollows), the Contributors and Guests report issues of their own in the projects where they hold a role and comment under them (reports), the Contributors change the title and tags of what they reported (contributorChanges; a Contributor cannot change a status, so none is tried), the Team members change statuses under the workflows, many of them on followed issues (teamStatusChanges), and about five hundred small files are added to issues and comments (files: pictures as PNG or JPEG and one-page PDFs, generated so that no two are the same file, by bb_files::fixtures::varied_picture and varied_pdf). The files are kept in the files/ folder of the data folder, and the previews are made by the job runner (Ctx::run_due_jobs, with PreviewCommand::in_process), so every file has its preview when the sample is done. (3) At the end the notifications come from the sample's own changes (the reader of the outbox, run by the same run_due_jobs), and the Viewers, Guests and Contributors mark readPercent of theirs as read. The counts are those of issues.work in tools/dev/sample.json, scaled like the issues (WorkPlan::counts, the one place both the program and the judge read them). The dump has a part issues.work: the workflows (statuses, changes, changes that ask), the projects with a workflow of their own, the files (pictures, PDFs, on comments, previews), the notifications (by kind, by the role of the person, read, and the ones a Guest got about an issue they did not report: none), the reports by role, the status changes of the team, the changes of Contributors and the follows of Viewers. The dump lists the people an issue is assigned to by label, since the order of their random IDs is not part of the organization. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (WorkPlan::judge in bb-dev-words, the tests m3_f111_…, att_04_…, wf_04_… of bb-sample).
  • Working hours and time (M6 WP-12): Maker::work_hours (time_work.rs of bb-sample) goes on after the people worked together, all through the use cases the screens call. Before the walk it adds the choices of Cost center (a number and a name each; the field starts empty) and an Estimated time to a third of the issues, spread evenly. It reads Activity and Cost center by the marks of the starter fields and takes the IDs of their choices from the fields, never by hand. The walk lets sessions idle for a day (an administrator changes Sign out after no activity for the walk and resets it after, so a person is signed in once a day, not at every tap), sets the clock back to the first of the last 13 weeks (time.weeks, scaled to a small sample, at least two) and moves it forward day by day, through the one helper World::move_clock_to that the other stages use too. Every employee (Administrators, Project leads, Team members and Contributors, without the people who sign in with a code app; a small sample takes the first few, the people of the demos first: time.employeesAtLeast) works their days in their own time zone: Start work day, Start break and End break, End work day at moments of their own, taps of the same use cases as the buttons, and a few time entries booked after the day with Add time, each with Activity and Cost center (about 20,000 entries in all; time.entries). The record is 13 weeks, not 26: the full sample takes about 17 minutes with 26 weeks and the time part has to stay near five (measured on a sample of 2,000 issues: a booking costs about 5.6 ms, a tap 4.2 ms and a sign-in or its reuse 3.6 ms, so the weeks are what to cut). Some days are on leave (leavePercent) and some break a rule (ruleBreakingPercent: a day of twelve hours, or a long day without a break), so the timesheet has warnings to show. After the walk some real past days are changed with a reason through change_work_day: by the person themselves (changedByPerson) and by Hana, who holds HR through the group Payroll (changedByHr); no stage gets round the rule that asks for the reason. A few Team members leave their timer running on an issue (runningTimers). The counts are those of time in issues.work of tools/dev/sample.json, scaled like the issues (TimePlan::counts, the one place both the program and the judge read them). The dump has a part issues.work.time (work days, time entries and how many have Activity and Cost center, the days changed with a reason by the person and by HR, issues with an estimate, running timers), counted in the events and the store. A time entry is dated on a day that may be before its issue was made: the sample books on any issue the person may book on. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (TimePlan::judge in bb-dev-words, the test time_01_… of bb-sample, which also reads the days back as the people would: some days carry a warning and some show Changed, Hana reads the days of Ben and finds Ana in Working hours of others, Ben is refused both).
  • The check: cargo xtask dataset sample --check makes the organization twice on SQLite and twice on PostgreSQL from one seed into target/sample-check/ and compares the canonical dumps. The dump leaves out what is random by design (IDs, password hashes, secrets and the hashes of the security log) and replaces each ID by a label that counts the records of a kind in the order they appear (person#3), so it still says which events and entries are about the same record. The run fails when two dumps differ, when an address is not under bugaboo.example, when a name is not a given name and a family name of the list, or when a password, secret or access key of sign-in.txt is found in any other file of a run (the database, the keys, the log files, the dump, what the program said). The dump also holds a part issues: for each project the issues of each type, status and priority, the sub-issues, the relations of each kind with the longest chain of blocks and the number of circles, tags, labels, the values of each own field, the comments (and how many were edited) and the locks and drafts left behind, and the run fails when they are not the plan of tools/dev/sample.json scaled to the issues asked for, within issues.tolerancePercent (IssuePlan::problems in bb-dev-words, which the tests of bb-sample ask as well). The dump also holds the groups with their members, the roles with how many people hold each, the projects with their leads, every row of Who has which role and the levels projects and custom roles set; the run fails when a group or project of this section is missing, when a role of the mix below is missing or held by another number of people, or when a project has no Project lead. The rules and their failing and passing examples are in xtask/src/checks/test_sample_data.rs and tools/checks/fixtures/TEST-SAMPLE-DATA/.

Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (cargo xtask ci runs it), ARCH-HTTP-EDGE (bb-sample is the second crate that may wire an adapter), SEC-SECRETS (no password in the repository).

People (50) and groups

  • 2 Administrators, 4 Project leads, 30 Team members, 8 Contributors, 3 Viewers, 2 Guests, 1 HR (Hana Weiss), plus 2 agents of one person (agents come with AI-30, M7).
  • Groups: Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA, Support, Docs, Management, External, Payroll. Every Team member is in one of the first six, every Viewer in Management and four Contributors (Ana is the first) in External, and Hana in Payroll.
  • Who has which role (made in M2, shown by Check access): the second Administrator and 18 of the 30 Team members for the whole organization; the other 12 Team members only through the groups Backend, Frontend, Mobile, QA and Docs (a group gives its role on its projects); the Viewers through Management for the whole organization; the Contributors in External on Website, the other four on Mobile app and Operations; the Guests one each on Website and Mobile app; one Project lead for each of the four projects; and one No access (Ben Hale on Android). Hana holds HR through the group Payroll, for the whole organization: she sees the working hours of others (the sample's own, M6).
  • Two custom roles: Support agent (a Team member without Cost center, given to the group Support on Operations) and Security reviewer (needs two-step sign-in; the five people who have a code app hold it on Operations).
  • Cost center is hidden from Contributors, and Guests see no authors or mentions, on Mobile app; Website keeps the starting rules, so the M2 exit demo has something to change.
  • Generated names from a mixed international name list; e-mail addresses under the reserved domain bugaboo.example, so nothing can ever reach a real inbox.
  • Each person has a time zone, some have passkeys, two-step sign-in or access keys. Two people are already removed (Former user labels) to test GDPR flows.

Projects (4, two with sub-projects) — about 10,000 issues

ProjectShort nameIDsSub-projectsIssues
Mobile appAPPrandomiOS (IOS), Android (AND)≈ 4,800
WebsiteWEBcountingShop (SHOP), Blog (BLOG)≈ 3,000
OperationsOPScounting—≈ 1,800, including restricted security issues
HandbookDOCcounting—≈ 400, mostly documents and tasks

What's inside

  • Issues over the last 18 months (dates are shifted at generation time, so the data always looks current): Bug 45 %, Task 30 %, Feature 20 %, Goal 5 %; realistic status ages, priorities and labels; own fields (Severity, Platforms, Customer); about 2 % restricted issues.
  • Sub-issues under goals, and about 3,000 relations of every kind, including chains deeper than four steps and one deliberate blocks circle (to test the warning).
  • Releases: three per project, one in the past, one current, one planned.
  • Comments: about 30,000, with mentions; some edited.
  • Files and documents: about 500 small generated attachments (images, PDFs), 60 pages and 20 files with several versions each.
  • Time: about 20,000 time entries with activities and cost centers, the last 13 weeks of working hours for every employee (time.weeks, including some broken working-time rules), and a few running timers.
  • Configuration: workflows for each issue type, field permissions (for example Cost center hidden from Contributors), Who sees people set for Guests, fields excluded from AI, saved searches, dashboards, two custom themes.
  • States worth testing: an edit lock held by someone, a pending conflict, a closed month, a person with a removal in progress.

The M2 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m2-exit-demo.spec.ts runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M2/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<light|dark>.png). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample (it prints where sign-in.txt is; sign in as Ada Brandt, the first line):

  1. Organization settings › Roles & permissions: make the role Reviewer from a copy of Viewer and tick See how the server is doing.
  2. Website › Project settings › Field permissions: for Contributor set Cost center to Hidden. Mobile app has it hidden already; Shop and Blog show it hidden "from Website".
  3. Website › Project settings › Who sees people: for Guest set Assigned to to Hidden; the preview now says Someone.
  4. Website › Project settings › Check access: pick Ana Moreno and read why she is a Contributor (through the group External) and that Cost center is hidden from her. Pick Ben Hale in Android to read that No access wins over his role.
  5. Sign out; sign in as the Guest of Website (see dump.json, the row with the role Guest on WEB) and as Ana: the tree shows Website with its sub-projects only, and the settings pages and Mobile app are not found.

The M3 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m3-exit-demo.spec.ts (the steps are in web/app/e2e/support/demo-m3-*.ts) runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M3/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png, ten steps, four themes). It starts from two changes an administrator and a Project lead make through the API (the form of the Website gets Assigned to and an own field Cost center for everybody but Guests, because Cost center is a field of time entries until M6; Guests see no names of assigned people). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample:

  1. A Guest of the Website makes a bug with the short form (title and description, no priority, no person, no cost center).
  2. A Team member makes a bug with the full form: priority, Cost center, and a colleague assigned.
  3. The Team member relates that bug to two issues of the Website (blocks).
  4. The Team member takes the Guest's bug (assigns the colleague, writes the cost center); the Guest opens it and reads Someone for the colleague, with no Cost center. A Guest sees only the issues they made (the spec asserts it: the Team member's bug is not found by the Guest).
  5. The Team member edits the description; an administrator opens the same issue in a second browser and is told who is editing, presses Edit anyway and saves; the Team member's text is kept and offered with Compare and save.

The M4 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m4-exit-demo.spec.ts (the steps are in web/app/e2e/support/demo-m4-*.ts) runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M4/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png, seven pictures of six steps, four themes). It starts from what an administrator and the Guest do through the API: a mail server that takes the e-mail (BUGABOO_MAIL_BATCH_SECONDS is two, so the e-mail comes while the test waits), the Guest of the Website given a role in Operations, the field Customer and who is assigned hidden from Guests, and a bug the Guest reported in Operations, whose e-mail for what they follow is on. The workflow of Operations is the one the sample made (Open to In progress asks for Assigned to). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample:

  1. A Team member opens the Guest's bug in Operations: Open.
  2. Start working opens a small window that asks for who does the work; the Team member names a colleague and saves: In progress.
  3. The Team member pastes a screenshot onto the bug (the row and its preview), and writes the customer.
  4. Mark as done: Done.
  5. The Guest opens Notifications: the bug and its changes are there, without the customer, the colleague (the Guest reads someone) and the name of the Team member (the Guest reads Someone (Team member)).
  6. The e-mail has come to the Guest too, without the customer and without the names; its link opens the bug.

The M5 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m5-exit-demo.spec.ts (the steps are in web/app/e2e/support/demo-m5.ts) runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M5/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png, seven pictures of six steps, four themes: step 3 also shows the last list behind the mistake). It starts from the saved searches of the sample (Saved searches of the sample below). By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample:

  1. A Team member searches for priority is high in Simple search: the list has issues and the count line says how many.
  2. Advanced search shows the same text; back to Simple search and again to Advanced search loses nothing.
  3. Ana Moreno, a Contributor of Website through the group External, writes customer is "Alder Street Bakery" in Advanced search: Customer is hidden from Contributors, so the box says "There is no field called "customer"", in the words of a field that does not exist (customex gets the same words). A Team member who may read Customer is answered.
  4. The searches the sample saved reach the people they are shared with: a Team member of Frontend finds Questions of customers (it reads Customer) and opens it; Ana is offered High priority, not done but never the one that reads Customer.
  5. Website shows High priority, not done as its list: its filters stand in the bar when the project opens.
  6. Quick search finds an issue of the sample by its title and opens it.

The hidden field of the demo is Customer, an own field that Contributors cannot read (the lead), and not Cost center: until M6 that is a built-in field of time entries which no search reads yet, so it would not show the answer of an unknown field. That the run on 1 M issues meets its budget is the nightly benchmark (Speed on 1 M issues).

The M6 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m6-exit-demo.spec.ts (the steps are in web/app/e2e/support/demo-m6.ts, demo-m6-hours.ts and demo-m6-people.ts) runs it in cargo xtask ci, on a phone and a computer, with axe in the four themes at every step; with BB_SCREENSHOT_DIR set the same run takes the pictures of the review page (M6/demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png, ten pictures of six steps, four themes). It starts from the sample: Ana Moreno (a Contributor on Website), Ben Hale (a Team member) and Hana Weiss (HR, through the group Payroll), and the working hours the sample recorded. By hand, with cargo xtask dev --sample:

  1. Ana starts her work day, starts the timer on an issue of Website, and stops it: the window Stop timer has Activity and Cost center (the timer's start is moved back so the window has a time to book), and Save time books it.
  2. Ana takes a break and ends her day with the buttons of the work day.
  3. The timesheet of a week with a long day (the day was typed afterwards, from six to seven in the evening) says it in the warning color.
  4. Ana changes the end of yesterday to 18:35 and gives her reason; the day shows Changed, and its history says who, when, what and why. On a phone, one day at a time, the same change is made through the same use case.
  5. Ben, who does not hold See working hours of others, is told there is no such page, and the menu has no entry.
  6. Hana opens the week of Ana in Working hours of others and sees its days; with Totals only switched on by an Administrator she sees the total of the week and nothing else.

Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the sample the demo runs on).

Saved searches of the sample (M5 WP-10)

The plan is issues.work.savedSearches of tools/dev/sample.json and the stage searches.rs of bb-sample makes them through the use cases after the people have worked together: eight searches by people of every role, private and shared with groups and with Website, one that Website shows as its list, and one that reads the own field Customer, which the stage hides from Contributors (hiddenFromContributors). A search that is shared with a group is made by an Administrator, because sharing with a group needs Manage groups or Share searches for the whole organization, which the roles of the sample give to nobody else. qry_06_every_role_saved_a_search_and_the_shared_ones_reach_only_who_reads_them reads the lists of every person of the sample back through the use cases on both databases: every search is in the list of its maker, the ones shared with a project reach a Contributor, none that reads Customer does, and the project list is the one the plan chose.

AI and agents of the sample (M7, part 6)

Part 6 of the sample (bb-sample, WP-13) is made through the use cases after the saved searches and before the working hours (ai_setup.rs, agents_work.rs; the numbers and names are the ai part of issues.work in tools/dev/sample.json):

  • AI is on for the organization. The provider is a made-up address under .example.test that never answers, so nothing leaves the computer (the browser tests put the test fake, a model on this computer, in its place); because the address is not on the local network, an administrator confirms the agreement. Website and Mobile app have AI on, Operations has it off. The project Handbook and the built-in field Time spent are Never sent to AI, and so are the own fields Cost center and Customer (marked through the change of the field, as its page does); both also stay hidden from Contributors. Send names of people stays off.
  • Two agents of one person, Fixer and Sorter, both of Ben Hale (a Team member), each with an agent key. The keys are written to sign-in.txt as comment lines that start with agentKeyMark (#agent), so a reader of the people skips them, and nowhere else.
  • Hand-overs in every state of agent work on nine issues of Website (and its sub-projects): Waiting for the agent, Agent working, Waiting for you with a question and with a plan, Ready for review (with a comment of the agent and a passed check), Agent gave up, Stopped (a hand-over of one day that ran out: the work happens ten days before the end of the sample and the clock then moves two days on, so the queued jobs run), and two reviewed ones, one accepted after a question, an answer and a sent-back attempt, and one thrown away.
  • One standing rule of Sorter over the saved search New bugs in Website, by proposals only, ending in 90 days (the most a rule may last unless the organization allows rules that never run out), with its matches written down; and, from WP-14, one rule of Sorter over Crashes in Website that hands over what it finds, with its hand-overs and their limits.
  • One AI app (Claude Code) allowed by a Contributor at the consent step, with a session, so the run page has one to show.

Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA. The dump has the part issues.work.ai, and AiPlan::judge (bb-dev-words) holds it against the plan and the rules of ADR-0029: AI on with the agreement confirmed; the projects and fields of the plan marked; two agents of one person with a key each; no agent holds a role or is Assigned to anything; no piece of agent work is on an issue its person cannot change (Check access as an administrator asks it); every state of agent work, a question and a plan waiting, an answer, a sent-back, an accepted and a thrown-away attempt; standing rules that hold no list of changed fields, name no field of people and end within the longest end the setting allows (90 days, or none where the sample allows it), a rule that hands over only hands over issues it found and of which the agent is not over its limit; one AI app of a Contributor; and every comment an agent wrote has the mark Written by an agent that names that agent. The tests are ai_30_… and ai_32_… in crates/bb-sample/src/tests/ai.rs, on both databases.

The M7 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m7-exit-demo.spec.ts runs the exit demo of 04-milestones (M7) with an MCP client inside the test and the fake provider, with pictures in the four themes on a computer and a phone. By hand (M7-Q9), the review page shows how to try it with the real things:

  • A real AI app: cargo xtask dev --sample starts the server on the sample; one command adds it to Claude Code as an MCP server (claude mcp add with the address cargo xtask dev prints). Claude Code registers itself (its return address is on the computer), the browser shows the consent step, and the app works as the person who allowed it.
  • A real provider: in Organization settings › Connections › AI, Set up the assistant with the maintainer's own Anthropic key (typed in the page, stored as a secret in the local data folder under target/, never in Git) after the agreement step, or a local model through the OpenAI-compatible choice.
  • The sample starts with AI on and the fake provider, so nothing leaves the computer until the maintainer changes the provider.

The goal with people (M8, part 7)

Part 7 of the sample (bb-sample, timeline_work.rs; the numbers and names are issues.work.timeline of tools/dev/sample.json) is made through the use cases after the working together and before AI (plan_the_goal):

  • The people. Lea Fischer and Noah Weber take the place of two Team members the seed made, after everything else was drawn from the seed, so the roles, the groups and the issues stay as the seed made them; only their names differ (an address of theirs is never drawn for anybody else). With Ben Hale they are the three people who plan in Mobile app.
  • The goal. Mobile app 2.0 has a due date; six issues of the type Task sit under it with start and due dates, estimates and three dependencies of blocks (Login screen before Profile page, Profile page and Push notifications before Release build). Days are counted from the first Monday after the end of the sample, so the plan lies ahead of the day the sample was made on.
  • Work times. The organization counts the public holidays of Bavaria. Lea works Monday to Friday with 6 hours a day (not the start values, so her usual work days are stored) and has a share of 100 % in Mobile app; nobody is away. One issue carries Lea's own estimate (Takes me …), set by Lea herself.
  • The check. plan_12_the_sample_plans_mobile_app_2_0_with_lea reads the dump on both databases and holds the part issues.work.timeline against the plan (bb-dev-words, sample_timeline.rs): dated issues in days before the due date of the goal, the dependencies, the holidays, Lea's usual days and share, no away time and the one own estimate.
  • The large dataset dates a share of the issues of the first project and its sub-projects (large.datedPercent, datedDays, datedLongestDays) with a start date, a due date and an estimate, from a random stream of their own (large_dates.rs), so the timeline of the biggest project has a page of bars to draw.

The M8 exit demo on the sample

web/app/e2e/m8-exit-demo.spec.ts runs the exit demo of 04-milestones (M8, with the answer to M8-Q3) on the sample, with pictures in the four themes on a computer and a phone (<folder>/M8/exit-demo/<step>-<phone|computer>-<theme>.png): Ada plans Mobile app 2.0 by dragging a bar (on a phone, which never drags, the step looks at the same plan); a week away of Lea grows her bars around it (computer) and the list of warnings says that Login screen now ends after the due date of the goal; a share of 50 % makes her bars longer again; as Lea an issue takes 10 days and shows as Lea's own estimate; given to a colleague it goes back to ×1 (as estimated); and a theme for everyone that is hard to read is refused, named, fixed and saved. Speed on the sample

web/app/e2e/perf-issues.spec.ts (the Playwright project speed, which runs every file perf-*.spec.ts after every other project, one test at a time, so nothing competes for the computer; by hand --project=speed --no-deps; M5-F98: the search page test used to run beside the whole suite and reached 100.6 ms) measures the reads of an issue page (the issue, its relations, sub-issues, related issues, history, tags and labels, follow and followers, asked all at once as the browser does) and the first pages of every project's list on the ten thousand issues, then the same with ten people writing comments and one reading, and the preview of a move. PERF-01 is the 95th percentile under 100 ms, with the program the tests run against (BB_SERVER_BIN names another build); the numbers go to test-results/perf-*.json. On the sample, in a debug build: pages 17 ms, lists 17 ms, a comment with ten writers 53 ms (release: 8, 6 and 30 ms; the numbers of M3 were 38, 44 and 64 ms in a debug build and 18, 17 and 39 ms in a release build, before the role of a person was looked up only for a viewer who sees roles). M4 WP-10 adds three tests of the same kind, all against the budget, with the numbers of the 95th percentile in a debug build and a release build: perf_01_issue_page_with_files_… (the reads of the page and the files and what may be added to them, on 200 issues of which 40 got three more files: 48 ms in a debug build, 10 ms in a release build), perf_01_notifications_page_… (the number on the menu, the first page of 50 and the two after it, for ten Team members of the sample who have thousands of notifications each: 52, 39 and 70 ms in a debug build, 16, 13 and 24 ms in a release build; before the pages were read with one statement for each row and the rights of each different person, they were 139, 81 and 120 ms in a debug build and 48, 30 and 50 ms in a release build) and perf_01_a_status_change_through_the_judge_… (100 status changes, also the ones that ask for who does the work: 25 ms in a debug build, 9 ms in a release build). The notifications are held to the rule of perf_05_… too (perf_notifications.rs): a page of forty rows, and the number for forty unread, run as many statements as five, because the issues and the comments of a page are read in one statement each and the rights of a person are evaluated for their role only for a viewer who sees people by their role (M3-F113: what is left is one statement for each different person on a page). The reads of the issue page do not include mention-choices, which the page reads only while somebody types after an @. perf_05_… (bb-server, both databases) counts the statements a read runs (Database::statements_run) and fails when an issue with many comments, relations, sub-issues and tags runs more than one with two, or a page of forty issues more than a page of five. In a test build (feature testing) the counter can also keep the text of every statement while a test asks for it (Database::capture_statements, take_statements; the Counter of perf_queries.rs does), so a failure of two windows that must be the same prints which statements one ran that the other did not (M5-F65). A page of notifications is counted for each kind of row on its own, comments and status changes: the newest rows of one reader pass have no order within a millisecond, so a page of mixed rows would count the mix by chance (M5-F107). The project speed has one retry: on a busy computer run it alone (--project=speed --no-deps), because a speed test that other work competes with measures the other work. The speed test of ten writers is M5-F101 (open: the history read is the slowest read of the page; under budget in 8 of 9 rounds alone). Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the sample the speed is measured on).

Large dataset

cargo xtask dataset large [--issues N] [--database sqlite|postgres] [--check] makes the PERF-01 scale: 500 people, 500 projects (the sample's four with their sub-projects, the rest in families of up to five), 40 groups and a million issues, on both databases unless one is named. The kinds of things are the sample's; the scale and the shares are written once, in large of tools/dev/sample.json (LargePlan in bb-dev-words). The datasets are kept in .work/dataset/<database> (an older one of the database is thrown away first), and the data of PostgreSQL is in the database bblarge of the throwaway cluster.

  • How it is made. bb-sample --large makes the first start, the fifty people of the sample, the sample's organization and what the issues stand on (issue types, own fields, labels, the workflow Operations) through the use cases, as the sample does, and adds the own field Cost center, hidden from Contributors. The rest is written in big transactions without the use cases (large*.rs of bb-sample): about 450 more people in the mix of roles of the sample (they cannot sign in: their password is thrown away), the rest of the groups, projects and role rows, and every issue (one that a Contributor or a Guest reported is assigned to the team and goes on like the others, so the team's changes and comments tell the reporter) with its comments (English and German), followers, tags, labels, sub-issue, relation, own-field values and file record (no file bytes; a download is not found). Every record that the use cases would have written an event for has its event, built by the same functions as the use cases' (bb_app::event_members, in the order they happened), and the counters of the projects are set at the end. The history of every issue and the notifications are then read from the events by the code a server runs; notifications are made for the newest 2% of the events (the older ones count as read long ago). The only thing the store adds for this is the feature dataset of bb-store (Transaction::set_issue_counter), which only bb-sample switches on. At the end the program makes the statistics SQLite chooses its indexes by from every row for every table it filled (Database::refresh_statistics, as the daily job statistics.refresh does on a server): the migrations analysed empty tables, and a dataset without exact statistics is searched with the wrong indexes (the nightly runs of M5: every search on SQLite at its 2 s limit). On PostgreSQL cargo xtask dataset large then runs VACUUM ANALYZE on the database (Postgres::vacuum_analyze in xtask/src/db.rs), so a measurement never starts before PostgreSQL's own upkeep has looked at the new rows.
  • Same every time. Every issue is drawn from the seed and its own number, so a run gives the same data whatever the size of the transactions. The IDs of the fifty people of the use cases are random, so they are left out of the fingerprint.
  • Time and working hours (M6 WP-12). The people who work (Administrators, Project leads, Team members and Contributors) book time on the issues they work on and record their days, in the same big transactions (large_time.rs). An issue that is assigned to somebody gets, on average, two time entries (timeEntriesPer100: 200 on 100 issues, none to five on each issue) by the first person it is assigned to, dated within twenty days of the making of the issue, each with a choice of Activity and of Cost center (the same starter fields and the same choices of the plan as the sample's, found once by time_fields.rs, which the sample uses too). For every person who works, the last workWeeks (13) weeks before the end of the dataset have their working days, a day on leave now and then (leavePercent) and a day that is too long now and then (longDayPercent), stored whole with the warnings of the working-time rules as the use case stores them (bb_core::working_time::warnings with the rules of the preset Germany). The events of an entry and of a day are built by the functions of the use cases (event_members::time_entry_booked and work_day_recorded), so the dataset does not hold a second copy of what an event says (SSOT). The check holds the time booked on every sampled issue against the one definition of time spent (the sum of its entries must be what spent_on_issues says) and fails in a run of --check when no sampled issue has a time entry. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the same rules as the sample's, for the large dataset).
  • Agent work (M7 WP-13). AI is switched on as in the sample (large_agents.rs of bb-sample), and Ben Hale, a Team member of the whole organization, gets the agents of large.agents in tools/dev/sample.json (three), each with a key that goes to sign-in.txt as a comment line like the keys of the sample. Of the issues of the projects that count their IDs (their readable IDs follow from the counter of the project), 1 % (workPercent) are handed over, a hundred in each hand-over, one agent after the other, for 90 days. Of every hundred of them an agent ended 10 with a result for the review (readyPercent), and each agent holds four attempts open, two being worked on and two waiting for an answer to a question (openPerAgent; an agent may work on only five issues at once); the rest wait for the agent. Two standing rules (rules) over the search ruleSearch in the biggest project have their match record, which the job of the rules writes. All of it is done by the use cases of agents, as the person and as the agent with its key, not by big transactions, so the data is made by the code that changes since, the search of agent states and My agents measure. The check holds that the agents have work and, from 100,000 issues on, that the standing rules found issues; the numbers by state go into the fingerprint. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the same rules as the sample's, for the large dataset).
  • The check. The program does not make the dump of the sample (it names the sample's four projects). It reads the database back and holds it against the rules of the sample that apply to the large dataset: every project that counts its issue IDs has a counter equal to its issues, the version of an issue is one more than the events that count a version up, every event about an issue has its row in the history of the issue, a Guest is told only about issues they reported, and neither Guests nor Contributors are told the value of Cost center. Every notification of a Guest or a Contributor that the check reads is held against the rules of what they are told. In a run of --check (the program is told --check) every event makes its notifications (checkNotifiedPercent) and the rules also fail when no notification of that kind of person was read, so they cannot pass without looking; a full build does not fail at 0. It prints a fingerprint of the issues, their comments (how many and their texts), their tags and their labels (of the issues that were held against their events). cargo xtask dataset large --check (a step of cargo xtask ci) makes 3,000 issues twice on each database with one start moment, and fails when a rule does not hold or the fingerprints differ. Enforced by: TEST-SAMPLE-DATA (the same rules as the sample's, for the large dataset).
  • Time and disk (this computer, release build, 1,000,000 issues): SQLite 18.7 minutes, 7.1 GB (the file and the keys); PostgreSQL 37.4 minutes, 9.0 GB (the database and the data folder). The check of the made dataset (20,000 issues held against their events) is part of those times.
  • The benchmarks. cargo xtask bench [--database …] starts a release server on the dataset of each database (a Node program, web/tooling/bench/main.ts, like cargo xtask load), signs in as the first Administrator, runs every scenario of web/tooling/bench/scenarios.ts 20 times as a warm-up and 200 times for the numbers, and writes p50, p95 and p99 of each to .work/bench/<date>.json, with how many runs were made (made) and how many were counted without one (skipped). A search that the server stops for taking too long (search.too-slow) counts as the time it really took (tooSlow says how many); once TOO_SLOW_IN_A_ROW runs in a row are too slow, the rest are not made and count as the slowest time seen, so a scenario that cannot finish shows plainly that it is far over its budget. The text index of a dataset is built once, before its first run (bugaboo search-index rebuild). A scenario is registered once, in scenarios.ts, with the name of its budget; the budgets are written once, in tools/checks/perf-bench.toml, and cargo xtask gen bench-budgets writes them as a TypeScript constant that the benchmarks and the speed tests (perf.ts) import. A run over a budget fails with the scenario, the number and the budget. Enforced by: PERF-BENCH (at commit time the file and the scenario list; every night the numbers).
  • The full run with benchmarks. There is no scheduled run (the maintainer, 2026-11-11): the benchmarks run by hand at each milestone exit, on a quiet computer. cargo xtask nightly runs cargo xtask ci, then dataset large for a database whose dataset is missing or was made for another migration than the newest (dataset large writes the name of the newest migration into the file made-for in the folder of the dataset; names are compared, not file times, which a checkout changes), then bench, and writes one log to .work/nightly/. It waits while another full run is on the computer: ci, bench and nightly take a lock first, a local port (fullRunLock in tools/dev/ports.json) that the system gives to one program at a time and takes back when it ends. dataset large (without --check) takes it too. A waiting run says which port it waits for and gives up with an error after 6 hours, so the night cannot hang. The lock goes with the program that holds it: a killed xtask frees it while the programs it started (the server, the database, a dataset run) may still be running; kill those as well before you start another run. cargo xtask nightly --install can still register a daily task (03:00, in the folder it is run in) with the scheduler of Windows, but none is installed.

Speed on 1 M issues

M7 adds three scenarios to the benchmarks (budgets in tools/checks/perf-bench.toml, PERF-BENCH, WP-13; web/tooling/bench/agent-scenarios.ts): agent-changes-since (the tool changes since of an agent, asked for the oldest mark, so it reads the bounded part of the log and the match record), search-agent-state (agent state is "waiting-for-the-agent") and my-agents (/api/v1/me/agents/work of the person who has the agents). The data is made by dataset large (see Agent work): three agents of one Team member hold the 1 % of the issues of the projects that count their IDs, about 3,300 issues each, and two standing rules over priority is critical and statusGroup is not Done have their match record. Numbers on 1,000,000 issues, release build, 95th percentile, against the budget of a page (100 ms) and of a search (300 ms). The scenarios take the three keys of the person's agents in turn and fail when a request is refused: a key may make 120 calls a minute and a person 240 (ADR-0042), and a refused request is fast, so the first numbers of this table (47 ms and 30 ms for agent-changes-since) were mostly refusals:

ScenarioSQLite p95PostgreSQL p95
agent-changes-since61.2 ms (first 109.3 ms, over; 331.1 ms at the first run)63.8 ms (first 154.0 ms, over; 476.1 ms at the first run)
search-agent-state42.2 ms174.8 ms
my-agents34.2 ms (73.7 ms at the first run)58.6 ms (119.9 ms at the first run)
issue-page (control)34.4 ms45.4 ms

agent-changes-since meets its budget since the M7 exit (M7-F127 done; best of three runs on a quiet computer on 2026-11-11, the numbers in the table; the nightly runs of 2026-11-10 and -11 gave 77.0 and 73.7 ms on SQLite, 84.1 and 79.5 ms on PostgreSQL). Any request through the harness costs about 30 ms (the control), so about 70 ms are left for the work of an agent. What was done first: the project of the issue is kept on the piece of work (migration 47), so the projects an agent reaches are one read of its work and no lookup of 3,300 issues; the settings of AI of all projects, the rights of the authors, the issues, the projects and the people of a page of the log are read together; a request looks at 400 events at the most. What was left on PostgreSQL was the count of reads: a request made about 170 transactions, each a round trip for BEGIN, its statements and ROLLBACK (the work was 40 ms in the database, the rest was waiting for them). The exit wave reads the matches and the work of a look together and looks up the key of an agent once for a message. The dataset took 41.8 minutes and 12.7 GB on SQLite and 61.1 minutes and 16.4 GB on PostgreSQL with the agent work, while other work ran on the computer.

M8 adds two scenarios (budget timeline of tools/checks/perf-bench.toml, 300 ms at the 95th percentile like a search, PERF-01; web/tooling/bench/timeline-scenarios.ts): timeline-biggest-project and timeline-biggest-project-by-effort (POST /api/v1/timeline for the first project, a page of rows, without and with Plan by effort). The data is made by dataset large (large.datedPercent of the issues of the first project have dates and an estimate: about 73,000 of the about 245,000 issues of the biggest project and its sub-projects). The numbers are measured by hand on a quiet computer at the exit of the milestone, when no other folder builds or tests. The first run (2026-11-16) took 780 and 862 ms on SQLite, 208 and 198 ms on PostgreSQL. Of the 710 ms of a page on SQLite, 650 ms were the count of Not scheduled yet (the issues of the search with neither date), which read every issue of the project from the table; the rows, the plan, the dependencies, the warnings and the work times took the other 60 ms. Migration 53 makes the index of the totals again with the two dates after its columns (issue_by_project_for_totals_and_dates), so the count reads the index alone (12 ms), and makes the statistics of the issues again at once: without them, until the round of the statistics five minutes after the start, SQLite chose badly and half of the counts of search-count stopped at the limit. The index holds no ID, for the reason of migration 36: an index with the dates and the ID (tried) made the timeline 64 ms and the totals 931 ms, but all three text searches stopped at their limit and search-agent-state went over its budget. The run at the exit (2026-11-16, release build, 95th percentile, on the datasets made that day and migrated to 53):

ScenarioSQLite p95PostgreSQL p95
timeline-biggest-project55.8 ms (780.1 ms before)54.5 ms (208.2 ms before)
timeline-biggest-project-by-effort57.4 ms (861.5 ms before)52.7 ms (198.2 ms before)
project-time-totals (known gap M6-F186)1,172.1 ms (1,846.5 ms before; limit 1,500)597.1 ms (602.7 ms before; limit 650)
many-changes-preview1,490.8 ms (5,060.2 ms before)2,737.1 ms (8,106.1 ms before)
search-groups-assigned-to (known gap M5-F89)612.1 ms231.3 ms
