Every other scenario is inside its budget on both databases; the whole run is in .work/bench/ of the folder it ran in.

The first numbers, on this computer, in a release build, at the 95th percentile (p50 and p99 in the file of the run), against the budget of 100 ms (PERF-01):

ScenarioSQLite p95PostgreSQL p95
issue-page: the eight reads of an issue page at once11.8 ms23.7 ms
list-big-project: the first page of the list of the big project (the first project of the sample, which the dataset ranks biggest; the benchmark fails when it has no more than one page)8.3 ms16.9 ms
list-small-project: the same for a small project (the one with the fewest issues among the last ten of the list, counted by reading its pages)8.2 ms13.0 ms
notifications-count: the number on the menu22.6 ms34.8 ms
notifications-page: the first page of 5020.2 ms30.3 ms
project-list: the list of projects (M3-F114)8.0 ms9.5 ms

M6 adds project-time-totals, the totals of the time of the big project (/api/v1/projects/{project}/time: the sums of Estimated time and Time left in one statement of the search of its list, and Time spent in one more, TIME-03), held to the budget of a page, and the issue page reads its time as a ninth read (/api/v1/issues/{issue}/time). The dataset has 1.4 million time entries and the last 13 weeks of working days for the people who work (Time and working hours, above). On it, in a release build at the 95th percentile (SQLite first, then PostgreSQL): the issue page with its time 35 and 47 ms, timesheet-week (the work days, the entries and the comparison of one week, read at once) 14 and 18 ms, issue-time-entries 6 and 7 ms. project-time-totals is over its budget and is a known gap (M6-F186, tools/checks/perf-bench.toml, one limit for each database: 1,500 ms on SQLite and 650 ms on PostgreSQL; 600 ms until 650 ms was accepted on 2026-11-16). The biggest project and its sub-projects have about 260,000 issues. Before M6 WP-12 the call was stopped by the limit of a search (2 s) on both databases: the sums of Estimated time and Time left read each issue whole from the table (500 to 900 ms on SQLite), and the minutes spent were summed with a lookup of the entries for each issue. Now the index of migration 36 (issue_by_project_for_totals: project, deleted at, estimate, time left) gives the sums from the index alone (22 ms on SQLite), and the minutes spent are the one sum of the time entries over the entries of the issues the search finds. What is left is one probe of the entries by issue for each of the about 260,000 issues of the biggest project and its sub-projects (a nested loop of 259,878 index-only scans on PostgreSQL): 790 ms at the median and 1.2 s at the 95th percentile on SQLite (2 of 200 runs still stopped by the limit), 434 ms and 515 ms on PostgreSQL. The index has no ID in it on purpose: with the ID in it SQLite was faster (285 ms at the median) but chose that index for the text searches too, which then took 2 s. A stored time spent for each issue would be a second definition (ADR-0035) and is not built; kept totals for each project or a project on each time entry belong to a later milestone. With the time entries of the dataset (from 2026-11-06) the nightly runs showed about 2.2 s on SQLite with no request counted (M7-F226): the first requests after the start of the server, on a cold file, were stopped by the limit of a search three times in a row in the warm-up, and the driver then gave up the scenario, counted runs and all. The warm-up is there to throw such runs away, so only counted runs may give up now (web/tooling/bench/measure.ts, measure.test.ts). Best of three runs on a quiet computer (2026-11-11): 753 ms on SQLite and 366 ms on PostgreSQL at the 95th percentile, inside the limits of the known gap. The large dataset of M8 gives an estimate to about 73,000 issues of the biggest project, and the first run on it (2026-11-16) took 1,846 ms on SQLite and 603 ms on PostgreSQL, over both limits. That is the work the dataset holds now, not code that changed: the worked-out Time left of an issue with an estimate needs the minutes spent on it, so the sums that were read from the index alone read those issues from the table (560 ms on SQLite), and the index gives the issues of a project in the order of their estimate, so the time spent, which reads every issue from the table for its ID, now reads close to a third of them out of the order of the table (1,000 ms against about 700 before). Since the exit of M8 the sums of Estimated time, Time left and Time spent are one statement (lengths_statement, ADR-0035, amendment M8), which reads each issue once, and the worked-out Time left reads the minutes spent on an issue once instead of twice: 1,172 ms on SQLite and 597 ms on PostgreSQL at the 95th percentile, inside the limits (on PostgreSQL by 3 ms: the two statements took 335 and 477 ms there, the one statement about 550 ms, without parallel workers, because a correlated read of the entries keeps the plan in one process). That left 3 ms of room under the old limit of 600 ms on PostgreSQL, so the limit was raised to 650 ms, accepted on 2026-11-16.

The number on the menu was the read that cost most (M5 WP-03 fix round, on a dataset made with the final code: 1,000,000 issues, the biggest project APP with 133,505 issues and the smallest with 117). Before the fix it was 45.9 ms on SQLite and 88.0 ms on PostgreSQL (100.5 ms on the first dataset, over its budget), the page 35.7 and 62.6 ms. The statement for the rows is fast (0.8 ms on PostgreSQL, from the index notification_by_recipient, before migration 29); the time went into the rights: a page named the issues of a hundred notifications in many projects, and for each project the person's rows, roles and levels were read again (about fifteen statements) and the project on its own. They are now read once for all the projects of a page (Ctx::evaluate_projects, the same decision as Policy::evaluate_with), and the test perf_05_the_number_on_the_menu_runs_as_many_statements_for_twelve_projects_as_for_two holds it (183 statements against 53 before). After: 22.6 ms and 34.8 ms, the page 20.2 and 30.3 ms.

The searches (M5 WP-04 to WP-10). The scenarios of the searches, at the 95th percentile against the budget of 300 ms (PERF-01), in a release build on the datasets of 1,000,000 issues (the first number is SQLite, the second PostgreSQL; the list of the big project is held to the budget of 100 ms of a page):

ScenarioSQLitePostgreSQL
list-big-project: the first page of the list of a project with sub-projects19.9 ms28.7 ms
search-complex, search-complex-sorted: status group is not Done and priority is High, with and without sort by created28.0 and 27.7 ms40.2 and 38.7 ms
search-count: the count line of the same search77.1 ms48.9 ms
search-groups-status: the groups by status95.2 ms62.2 ms
search-groups-assigned-to: the groups by Assigned to572.9 ms (over)272.5 ms
search-text-common-word (a word in 187,000 texts), -prefix, -and-filter, -rare-word198.5, 232.2, 189.1 and 84.3 ms164.2, 246.4, 254.1 and 233.9 ms

What cut them (M5-F46, F47, F48; before: 716 ms for the list of the big project, 1,176 ms for the common word on SQLite and the 2,000 ms of the limit on PostgreSQL):

  • A page is cut after its first rows of each stream. The first page over a few projects (two to sixteen in the sight, no text) is the first rows of each project, read from the index of the project and the creation, put together (branches in search/statements.rs): SQLite cannot merge the ordered ranges of several projects from one index. The order by title hits (the issues that have the words in the title come first, then the newest) is two streams, the issues with the words in the title and then the others, each cut after its first rows. Both are exact: what comes first never depends on a cap, and a cursor continues in the right stream. Each page keeps the same order on both databases (ARCH-DB-PARITY).
  • How the words are found depends on how many rows of the text index a word has (SET_ROWS_AT_MOST, 2,000), which a probe of the index counts first (text_rows_up_to, one row for each word and stream, cut at that number, so it costs the same for a common and a rare word): the issues of the rarest word are made once and asked about the other words (Form::Driven), else each issue is asked in turn, which stops at the first rows (Form::Each); a count or the groups make the whole set (Form::Set). A search for a rare word is as quick as before, and for a common word it stops early.
  • The groups of a field with many values (assigned people, tags, labels, own fields) read the issues once with the rows of their values joined by LEFT JOIN (Rows in search/source.rs); the group without a value is the issues the join has no row for, so there is no second scan.

search-groups-assigned-to is still over its budget on SQLite. About 116,000 issues match, and SQLite reads the whole table of the issues for the ID of each issue it joins to the people assigned to it: of 590 ms, 500 ms are that read (the count of the same search, from the index of the filters alone, takes 75 ms; the lookups in the index of the assigned people are the rest). What was tried in M6 (M5-F89, F169, F170), measured on the 1 M datasets made with VACUUM ANALYZE (the computer was not quiet, so each was held against the old statement in the same minutes; the times are the best of several runs, warm): the IDs from an index that holds them, in their order and made once (a MATERIALIZED table of the IDs, with the ID at the end of the index of the filters): 270 ms against 700, but with the ID in that index SQLite asks it again for every issue the text search finds, and all four text scenarios stopped at their 2 s limit, as migration 23 had seen; only the rows the condition finds, through their place in the table (rowid IN (…)): 460 ms against 700, but on a cold file the reads all over the table took the 2 s limit three times in a row and the run failed where the full read passed; parallel slices of the projects on four or eight connections: no faster (520 and 600 ms), the connections wait for each other; counting rows instead of distinct issues: 4% on SQLite. Only the last is in the product; kept counts, or an index with the IDs that the text search is kept from, are the next step (M6 follow-up). The group counts its rows where an issue has a value once (the key of the table is the issue and the value: the people assigned, the tags, the labels; Repeats in search/source.rs), which on PostgreSQL lets the parallel workers count: 115 ms against 160 ms for the statement as the server prepares and runs it (a read-only transaction with its time limit, a quarter less). The scenario itself took 280 ms in the nightly run of 2026-10-31; in the benchmarks of M6 on a busy computer the request took 320 to 420 ms at p50 while its statement took 115 to 160, so most of the time is the rest of the request (the session, the rights and the names of the 340 people of the groups), which is where the next cut on PostgreSQL is. The entry of the known gap stays, with its limit of 700 ms; PostgreSQL is held to the budget. The budget stays 300 ms; the scenario is measured on the 1 M dataset and the nightly run tells it as a known gap and fails it only over its own limit (p95_ms_at_most), and tells when it meets its budget again so the entry can go. The one place that says so is [known_gaps] in tools/checks/perf-bench.toml (database, follow-up and reason), which cargo xtask bench reads. The limit is above the budget of the scenario, which the check holds.

The preview of 5,000 issues (M3-F133) and what a request costs before its data (M4-F137). many-changes-preview, the preview of a change of status to the most issues one change names (5,000, the first of the big project), has a budget of its own, preview of 8,000 ms (tools/checks/perf-bench.toml), because it judges every issue with the use cases of a single change: 3.0 s on SQLite and 6.7 s on PostgreSQL (before: 4.2 and 9.0 s). Each issue cost 10 statements, 4 of them the definitions of the own fields, which the same request read again for every issue; the request now reads them once (Ctx::field_catalogue, kept in Known and dropped by the use cases that change a field or a choice), which left 6 for each issue (the project of the address read by its short name, twice, the issue, the issue again as the change reads it, who is assigned, the chain of the project). On PostgreSQL every statement is a trip to the database of about 0.2 ms, so these trips were the largest part of the time (M5-F169). Since M6 the project of an address and the chain of a project are read once for the request (Ctx::project_by_address, Ctx::chain_of, kept in Known and dropped by every write of a project, which goes through Ctx::record_change; prj_03_a_request_that_moves_a_project_reads_its_chain_again), which leaves 3 for each issue: p50 4.6 to 3.4 s on SQLite and 8.6 to 3.2 s on PostgreSQL (p95 5.3 to 3.7 s and 9.3 to 3.9 s) on the same datasets, on a busy computer (the nightly numbers before were 2.9 and 6.1 s). perf_05_each_issue_of_a_preview_costs_the_same_few_statements holds the 3 and the 31 of a preview of one issue (42 before M4-F137). The statements every request pays were counted for a page of notifications, before M4-F137: the session 7 (the session, the person, the settings twice, the second step, the passkeys, whether a role asks for a second step), the rights of the person 20 (8 for the organization and 12 for the project of the page: the groups, the assignments, the roles, their permissions and their levels, and the IDs of the own fields, each read again for the project), the definitions of the own fields and the issue types 5, the catch-up of the reader of the outbox 2 and 7 for the rows (the page, the issues, the comments, the project, the workflows, a person, a setting). The largest block, the rights, read the rows of the person again for each place. Since the exit wave of M5 (M4-F137) a request reads them once: Ctx::evaluate takes the rows of the person, their roles and the levels of those roles for the organization and every project from the store in one snapshot (person_policy, 8 statements: the levels of each kind are one UNION ALL of the table of a role's own levels and the table of the levels set for projects) and, for each project, the one read that tells it is there and where it sits (project_chain); the engine chooses what applies at each place (evaluation_from_person_policy, which is Policy::inputs_from_rows), so no rule moved and nothing is kept across requests. The rights of a page cost 9 statements instead of 20, on both databases: the fixed cost of a preview of one issue and of a page or the number of notifications went from 42 to 31, a list of a project from 58 to 44 (46 with its labels), a search with labels from 54 to 51, the number of notifications over twelve projects from 39 to 36, a page of saved searches from 40 to 36 (for a guest 43 to 40). A request that asks about the organization alone is no dearer than before (Which::At with no project reads the one table). Each further project of a request costs one statement (perf_05_the_reads_of_the_rights_do_not_grow_with_the_places_but_by_one_for_each), no longer fifteen; the level rows read grow with the projects the roles of the person have levels for (M5-F109). sec_03_every_place_of_a_request_is_decided_from_one_read_and_as_from_one_read_each (the test store) and sec_03_the_rights_read_once_decide_every_place_as_the_rights_read_for_each (both databases) hold the decision equal to the one made from a read for each place. A project that is not there is judged at the place of a project that is not there (place_of_address), not at the organization, so it costs the store the same reads as a project the person cannot see (prj_01_a_hidden_project_and_a_missing_one_cost_the_same_reads). At the exit of M8 the preview took 5.1 s on SQLite and 8.1 s on PostgreSQL at the 95th percentile (4.6 and 5.7 s at the exit of M7), and its time grew faster than its issues (0.55 s for 1,000 issues, 1.85 s for 2,500, 5.5 s for 5,000 on SQLite), while the statements stayed 3 for each issue and took 0.6 s of the 5.5 s: each issue took a copy of the values of the own fields of the whole selection that the preview had read ahead (ItemValues::only now hands out the values of the issues asked for). Since then: 1.5 s on SQLite and 2.7 s on PostgreSQL, growing in line with the issues.

The speed tests of the browser (perf_01_* in perf-*.spec.ts) run after the rest of the suite, one at a time (the speed project), so their numbers do not follow the load of the other tests (M5-F98).

A spec that belongs to one device carries it in its name: *-phone.spec.ts runs only in the phone projects and *-computer.spec.ts only in the computer projects (testIgnore in web/tooling/playwright.config.ts), so a test for one device is never a skipped test on the other (coding-standards §7).

Ten people at the same time

Concurrency is tested with 10 simulated people (an administrator and Team members of one project, made for the run), each in their own browser context (Playwright) or API client (cargo xtask load --people 10):

ScenarioWhat must hold
Three people try to edit the same descriptionOne gets the lock; the others see "… is editing"; Edit anyway moves the lock and keeps the first person's draft
Two people change the status of the same issue within a secondOne wins; the other sees the conflict message; nothing is half-saved
A lock holder's network dropsThe lock frees itself within a minute; their text is kept as a draft and offered with Compare and save
Ten people change different fields of one issueAll ten changes land (whoever was second presses Use mine); one event for each; the version counts up ten times
Ten people move issues through a workflow whose status change asks for who does the work (Ask for) and write an own field that Guests cannot see (M4 WP-10)Each status that was kept is the one the issue has; a change whose buttons were read before somebody moved the issue is refused, not half saved; the Guest, who reported one issue, is told only of that issue and no notification of theirs shows the hidden field
Ten people add files while others change the issueEvery file that was added is stored once on its issue, none is lost or doubled
Changing many issues while somebody edits one of themA lock covers only the long text, so the issue under edit changes too, and the editor's save lands afterwards with no conflict note (the status is another field); an issue whose text was saved after the preview is skipped and named, and the others change
Everyone drags cards on the same boardFinal board matches the event log; every person's screen shows the final state after refresh
Timers and working hours start and stop at the same timeNo double entries; working-time rules evaluated once per change
Two agents take the same issue at the same moment (M7)One take wins; the other is refused with the issue's newer version and starts nothing; one attempt, one run
An agent works while its person loses access (M7)The agent's next call is refused; its open work becomes Stopped; no change lands after the loss; Undo the run still works for the person who may undo it
Searches while others change dataResults respect permissions at every moment; no errors; latency within budget
Ten people plan at once (M8): they move the bars of five issues, two people to a barNo date is lost: each bar has the dates of the last move that was kept; a move that came second is told so and sent again on the newer version (Use mine); the versions run up one by one with one event for each
A warning is accepted while its bar moves (M8)An acceptance holds only the dates the person saw; the plan counts it only while the dates are the same, so the warning is back after the move
An away time is entered while the plan is read (M8)The days are stored once, and the next answer of the plan names them
Move it after is sent after somebody changed an issue it moves (M8)It is refused whole: nothing it names changes; on a fresh preview it is kept, and every issue it names moves

The load run and the invariants test run against both SQLite and PostgreSQL; the browser scenarios of ten Playwright contexts run on SQLite only, because each worker of the end-to-end tests starts its own server on its own data folder (ADR-0023) and a PostgreSQL database for each of them is not worth what it would add: the behaviour that differs between the databases (the conditional writes of the locks, the order of events) is what the load run and the invariants test cover on both. The short version (2 minutes) runs in CI; the long version (30 minutes, mixed workload) runs nightly and checks invariants afterwards: every change has an event, no lock outlives its lease, no text is lost.

The two ways to run them

  • Ten browsers (web/app/e2e/concurrent/): each person has a browser context of their own, signed in through the API (the sign-in has its own tests). The tests read what the people see (Saved, the "… is editing" note, Edit anyway, the conflict note with Use mine, Compare and save), never only timing, and wait for the answer of the server or for a note on the screen, not for a fixed time. The scenarios of the table above are iss_17_three_people_edit_one_description_and_the_first_text_is_kept, iss_17_a_lock_holders_network_drops_and_the_text_comes_back_with_compare_and_save, iss_17_two_people_change_one_status_within_a_second_and_one_of_them_is_told, iss_17_ten_people_change_ten_fields_of_one_issue_and_every_change_lands_once, iss_09_changing_many_issues_skips_the_one_changed_since_the_preview_and_names_it, which previews a change of status for four issues, lets one editor save the text of one of them, confirms the change and reads on the screen of the person that the issue is named and left alone while the others changed with one event each, and iss_09_changing_many_issues_changes_the_one_somebody_is_editing_and_their_text_is_saved_after, which previews the same kind of change, lets Ben hold the lock of the description with text that is not saved, confirms the change (all four issues change, Ben's too) and has Ben save: his text lands without Compare and save, and his issue has one status event and one text event (the preview and the change are previewManyChanges and applyManyChanges; web/app/e2e/support/many-changes.ts is the one place that knows their bodies). The scenario of the dropped network says which console lines it expects (tolerate) from the browser of the holder, and only while that browser is offline; every other console error, every uncaught error and every other browser stays checked. tolerate( may only be used in concurrent/locks.spec.ts and in mail-server.spec.ts and screenshots-notifications.spec.ts (where the one test of a wrong mail password, and the pictures of it, expect the 502 of mail.rejected, without cutting the network; TEST-CONCURRENT). The lock must free within the lease (60 seconds), plus the few seconds the page takes to look again; the time the test waits is made from leaseSeconds and heartbeatSeconds of the generated constants, never from a number of its own. The lock scenarios also run in the WebKit phone project.
  • cargo xtask load --people 10 [--minutes N | --nightly] [--database sqlite|postgres] (xtask/src/load/): the API at speed. xtask builds the program, starts the database of the run (the throwaway PostgreSQL for the second run) and runs the Node driver web/tooling/load/main.ts, which starts a server on the port loadTestServer and a data folder that xtask gave it, makes an organization (one project, six shared issues, Team members), lets the people change titles, edit descriptions under their locks (some editors vanish without letting go, some take the editing over), write comments and read, and writes what each person kept, was refused and read to a book (a JSON file). When the server has stopped, xtask runs bb-load-check on the book and the database of the run, which judges the invariants of the next section. The driver defines no invariant. Without --database it runs on both databases; tools/dev/load.json holds the defaults (ten people, two minutes, thirty for --nightly) and the name of the variable that carries the database address. cargo xtask ci runs it.
  • Ten people who plan (plan_03_ten_people_plan_at_the_same_moments_and_the_rules_hold in bb-server, both databases, and web/app/e2e/concurrent/planning.spec.ts, whose four tests are plan_03_ten_people_move_bars_at_the_same_moments_and_no_date_is_lost, plan_13_a_warning_accepted_while_its_bar_moves_comes_back, plan_11_an_away_time_entered_while_the_plan_is_read_shows_on_the_next_answer and plan_13_move_it_after_while_someone_changes_an_issue_it_moves_is_refused_whole). The rules are crates/bb-load-check/src/plan.rs, with a unit test for each. The driver of cargo xtask load does not run these cases yet.
  • Ten people and their agents (test_concurrent_ai_30_ten_people_and_their_agents_hold_the_rules in bb-server, both databases, and the second part of the Node driver web/tooling/load/agents-run.ts, on both databases of cargo xtask load): ten people each hand an issue to their agent, which takes, reports, changes a priority it was allowed to change, asks and submits over /mcp while its person answers and reviews; two agents take one issue at the same moment; an agent goes on after its person lost access. The agents, their people and their issues are made before the others start, because a search for everything judges the issues of the run.
  • Against the database (test_concurrent_invariants_hold_after_a_run in bb-server, both databases in the Rust tests step, which runs cargo nextest run under cargo xtask db run): ten people change four issues together over HTTP while the clock of the test runs on until the last person is done, so leases really run out (a person who types for longer than the lease waits for the clock, not for real time), and then the invariants are read from the database by the same function the load run ends in.

Invariants after every run

They are written once, as the function check of the crate bb-load-check (judge.rs): the test of the server builds its book in memory and calls it, cargo xtask load calls it through the program bb-load-check with the book of the driver. Nothing else defines them (SSOT).

  1. Every change has an event: the events about each issue count each version from 2 up to its version once, one event for each change that was kept (events about a lock taken over or let go count no version), and there is one event for each comment.
  2. Versions only go up, one at a time: the versions of the kept changes of an issue are 2 up to its version, each once, and what one person reads of an issue never goes down.
  3. No lock outlives its lease: no lock row ends later than the lease (60 seconds) from now, nobody holds a lock when the leases are over (in a load run nobody starts to edit under a lock in the last 70 seconds), and after the purge no row of a lock is left. One definition, used while the people work (the test of the server) and at the end (both).
  4. No text is lost: a save that was refused (lock lost, taken over, text changed) is the draft of the person at once, the heartbeat draft of an editor who vanished is still there after the lease, and the description is the text of the last save that was kept.
  5. The title is what the last kept title change set (M3-F93), and the status what the last kept status change under the workflow set (WF-01); a change that is lost or half saved is found.
  6. The files of an issue are the ones that were added to it, none more and none fewer (ATT-01).
  7. No notification shows what its person cannot see (SEC-06): a Guest is told only of the issues they reported, and no notification of a Guest keeps a field that is hidden from Guests, neither a built-in one that the starting role hides nor the own field the run hid. The run has nine Team members and one Guest, a project with a workflow of its own that asks for Assigned to on Open to In progress, and the own field Internal note, which Guests cannot see.
  8. Searches hold the rules while others change data (SEC-06, QRY-05): everybody searches now and then (a search for everything, one with a filter, one with words, and one that reads the own field hidden from Guests) and writes down what they were told. A search finds no issue the person cannot read (a Guest reads only what they reported), a search for everything finds exactly the issues the person reads with a count line that agrees, and the own field hidden from Guests is refused for a Guest and answered for everybody else. A run of two minutes makes about 1,800 searches.
  9. Agents hold the rules of ADR-0029 (M7 WP-13, agents.rs of bb-load-check): of agents that took one issue at the same moment exactly one was told it had it, and no issue has two attempts running; every event of an agent names an agent of the book and the person responsible for it, on an issue that was handed to that agent, and carries the run of its attempt; an agent whose person lost access kept no change after the loss and has no work that is not Stopped; and every run that was undone has, on each issue it changed, its undo event or the issue is named as skipped. The run has the eight Team members with an agent and an issue each, one more person who loses access, and one issue two agents take at once; some reviews accept, some send back first, some throw an attempt away.

Enforced by: TEST-CONCURRENT (the scenarios, the invariants test and the load step of cargo xtask ci are there and not switched off), TEST-EDIT-LOCKS (the browser scenarios of the locks).

Browser tests and the connections of the computer (M4 WP-03)

On Windows a computer that has no free ports or socket buffers left answers net::ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE, and a browser test that gets it fails (fixtures.ts counts every net::ERR_* as a defect, and no retry is added to hide it). The one exception to what counts as a defect is a failed load of a part of the app while the page is being left (a reload, a link to another address): the browser cancels what is still loading, and the app does not report that (web/app/src/shared/leaving-page.ts); every other error is reported, also then. A closed connection stays in TIME_WAIT for about two minutes, so what a run needs is the number of connections it closed in the last two minutes, not the number open. Three work folders that test at the same time share the computer.

What a run is measured by. The Playwright reporter web/tooling/connection-guard.ts looks at the connections of the computer during the run, one look after the other with a pause of a second between them (a look takes about 1.7 seconds on Windows; the next one is planned only when the one before has ended, the timer never keeps the process alive, and no look is made while the speed tests run, which measure on a computer that is otherwise idle; PowerShell's Get-NetTCPConnection on Windows, because netstat there prints the states in the language of the system; ss or netstat on Linux) and counts, for the ports of the workers' servers (e2eWorkersFrom to e2eWorkersTo of the folder's block), the connections in ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT. At the end of the run it prints the peak, writes the second-by-second counts to test-results/connections.csv and fails the run when the most it saw in TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT at once is over MOST_LEFTOVER_CONNECTIONS (web/tooling/connections.ts, the one place that names the limit). The sentence names the peak, the limit, the server and the spec its worker ran last. The limit is 1,800: a run needs about 1,250, and the run before the work package peaked at 1,989, so a fall back to the old way of testing is seen. One work folder never came near the ports that Windows gives out for connections (16,384), so the failure of three merges of M3 most likely needed several folders testing at the same time, which is why the guard looks at what one run needs. The summary also says how many connections in TIME_WAIT the whole computer had (the ones with a local port of the dynamic range, from 49,152), for information; it never fails the run. Above BUSY_COMPUTER_TIME_WAIT (3,000) the summary adds "Other work is on this computer", and when a test fails with net::ERR_NO_BUFFER_SPACE the reporter prints the count of the whole computer next to what the run left over, so a reviewer sees whether it was the run or its neighbours (M4-F22). The run fails too when any look failed or none was made (PowerShell, or ss or netstat on Linux, not working), so that nobody believes a guard that did not look; the summary says how many looks failed. The pure part (reading the lists, judging) is tested in web/tooling/connections.test.ts. Enforced by: TEST-CONNECTIONS (the reporter is in the Playwright config and fails the run, the limit is one named number, the tests of the guard are not switched off, and tests are run again only in the speed project).

What was measured. The full end-to-end run (about 700 tests, 16 workers, one work folder testing):

RunPeak in TIME_WAITIn CLOSE_WAITOpen at mostWhere
Before (readiness probes, one request context for each session)1,989060WebKit phone
After the readiness wait and the shared connections of the sessions1,918054issues-new.spec.ts, WebKit phone
After WebKit runs two tests at a time1,248056issues-editing.spec.ts, WebKit phone

Most of the connections are from WebKit, not from the helpers of the tests. One spec file alone shows it: issues-new.spec.ts leaves 16 connections in TIME_WAIT in Chromium (6 tests) and 438 in WebKit (the same 6 tests), and the project webkit-phone (20 tests in four files) alone peaks at 1,689, almost all of the peak of the whole run. On Windows, WebKit opens a connection for about every request of a page and closes it again (27 requests of the sign-in page leave 29 connections behind, against 2 for Chromium); the server keeps its connections alive (curl reuses one, and so does a Node client), so the cause is not in the listener and crates/bb-api/src/listener.rs is not changed. The project therefore runs two WebKit tests at a time (WEBKIT_WORKERS), which takes the peak from 1,918 to 1,248 and the run from 5.7 to 7.2 minutes (7.4 to 7.7 in cargo xtask ci).

What each task changed.

  • Readiness (web/app/e2e/support/ready.ts): the wait for a server asks GET /health/live over HTTPS with pauses of 50, 100, 200 … 1,000 ms instead of a raw TCP connection every 100 ms. A question that is refused leaves no connection behind, and one that is answered leaves one. A test with a server that answers late (web/tooling/ready.test.ts) asks at most seven times and the server sees one connection. In the measured run this was too small to show in the peak (a start has one successful probe either way).
  • Shared connections for the sessions of the API (web/app/e2e/support/session-transport.ts): every ApiSession and useKey script of a server goes over one pool of keep-alive connections of that server (closed when the server stops) and keeps the cookies of its own in a jar, so two people never share a sign-in. Before, each session was a Playwright request context with connections of its own that were closed at dispose. A session that was opened for a helper call is now free (openSession and useKey are no longer async). A connection that nobody used for 20 seconds is closed by the pool before the server's header timeout (30 seconds) would close it, and a GET or HEAD that meets a connection the server closed is sent once more; a request that changes something is never sent again, because nobody can tell whether the server took it.
  • Fewer server starts is not done, and the measurement says why it would not help: a start leaves about one connection (its readiness question), a few hundred of the two thousand. A server that is reset instead of restarted needs a route that exists only in a test build, which is product code (bb-server, an architecture decision) and not part of this package; a fresh data folder on the same process is not possible, because the server holds its data folder open. What the package keeps is what the work package asks for first: a spec cannot see what an earlier spec left behind. A worker starts a server on an empty data folder for every file, and isolation.spec.ts proves it: it makes a project and an issue, asks the worker for the server of another file, and finds the same port with the setup code accepted again and no project in it.
  • The guard above, and No hiding: no retries are added (the speed project keeps its one), and fixtures.ts still counts every net::ERR_*.
  • Showcase pictures (M2C-F104): the browser of every window stands at the moment the sample was made (sampleStartMs()), so "3 days ago" is the same on every run, and the address of the invitation is fixed. The few screens that show what the server makes in every run (a date and time, how long it runs, the link of an invitation with its secret, the hash of the security log) have those places painted over in their pictures (support/showcase-masks.ts, M4-F24), the link of an invitation is written the same way before the picture (its secret wraps at other places, so the box around it was another height), and the pointer is out of the page: two runs of the 212 phone pictures are now the same bytes.

Reading the numbers again. Run the end-to-end tests with npm run test:e2e (or cargo xtask ci), and read the last lines: Connections of the tests: at most N left over at once …. The seconds-by-seconds counts are in test-results/connections.csv.

Browser tests wait for what they depend on (M4 WP-18)

A test that is right on a quiet computer can lose a race in the full run, where 16 workers share the processors. Two such races were found only by cargo xtask ci, so a browser test waits, with a web-first assertion (await expect(…)), for the state its next step depends on:

  • Before it stops the page's clock (page.clock.pauseAt, page.clock.setFixedTime), it waits until the screen it tests has drawn. The page reads its data on timers, and a stopped clock holds them back (access-key-day.spec.ts).
  • Before a second window reads, it waits until the first window shows that the change is stored, not only that the text is on screen (concurrent/locks.spec.ts: the watcher reloads only after Save mine is saved).

No retry and no longer timeout is added to hide a race; the fix is the missing wait.

Nothing moves under the cursor: the measure (M8 WP-13)

A change a person makes may change only what they changed (UX §6.4). A browser test checks it with one measure, movementWhile in web/app/e2e/support/movement.ts; no spec has its own copy. While the action runs, and until every read of the API it started has answered and been drawn, it records in every frame the browser draws:

  • the browser's own record of layout shifts (PerformanceObserver with layout-shift, every entry, also those right after an input, which the browser leaves out of its own score; WebKit keeps no such record, so there the boxes are what holds);
  • the box of each named landmark (a CSS selector, or an element found by a locator and marked with landmarkOf; an element that is drawn afresh loses the mark and counts as gone), and the scroll of the page and of every part that scrolls;
  • whether grey shapes stood on the screen.

expectStill fails when a landmark moved by more than half a pixel (boxes are compared as the browser lays them out, not rounded: not even 1 px may move), when any layout shift above nothing was recorded, before or after an input, when a landmark went away, when grey shapes showed, or when the page or a part scrolled. What the action changes and what stands under it are named as follows: those landmarks may move once, in one step, when it grows, and a shift counts as theirs only when every element it moved stands inside one of them; a part that pushes them back and forth fails. A part whose scroll the action is meant to change (a form that starts again brings its first box into view) is named in scrolls. The wait for the reads counts only the requests seen after it began, so a read that started before cannot end it early. The landmarks of each screen are written once, in support/landmarks.ts, with what the person changes there; the nothing-moves*.spec.ts files hold the tests (ux_01_…), on a computer, a phone and the WebKit phone. A test measures from the person's action, not from the opening of a window or a page: it first waits until the screen is whole. The measure judges what the person sees: a landmark is compared by its edges that show in the window (a landmark with neither edge in view is compared whole, where it stands in its box when one scroll kept the view still), so one that changed only where it is out of view (a row came into the Details above the view, and the browser kept what is in view still by its scroll) has not moved; what grew wholly above the view pushes nothing in it, and two landmarks of one element count as one.

The first read has a measure of its own (support/first-read.ts, judged by first-read-judge.ts, tested without a browser): a script that runs before the app notes, once the browser has drawn each frame, where every part (data-part) stands, from the first frame of the page until every read of the API has answered and been drawn. A part laid out but hidden is not yet drawn. The judge fails a part that, once drawn in view, stands elsewhere, gets narrower or lower; grey shapes that go and content drawn in their place, and a part growing at its end, pass. nothing-moves-first-read.spec.ts holds every main screen to it, on a computer and a phone.

What the measure found shaped one rule of the query cache: the screen hears of a change of the cache in the turn it happens, not one timer later (notifyManager.setScheduler(queueMicrotask) in shared/query-client.ts). A change writes its new value and starts Saving… in one turn; with a timer between them the two reached the screen one frame apart, and what the change made larger grew twice (M8-F131).

The upgrade test

The migrations of a release can only be proven against a real older database, so every release upgrades a database that the program of the previous milestone made, on SQLite and on PostgreSQL, and checks that it reads the same afterwards (ADR-0046, decision 5). cargo xtask upgrade-test (xtask/src/upgrade.rs) does it, and cargo xtask ci runs it as a step, before each release too:

  • The previous milestone is the newest tag mN-done before HEAD, which git describe finds; no tag is written down anywhere, so the test moves on by itself when the next milestone is tagged.
  • One old program. The sample program (bb-sample) of that tag is built once, with optimisations, in a git worktree under .work/upgrade/ with a build folder of its own. Only the program is kept, in target/upgrade/<tag>/; the worktree and its build folder are deleted at once (about 1.3 GB), and so is the program of an older tag, so the disk keeps one file. Later runs find it there and build nothing.
  • The old data. On each database the old program makes the small sample organization, as cargo xtask dataset sample does (on PostgreSQL in the database bbupgrade of the throwaway cluster), with its sign-in file and its dump.
  • The upgrade. The driver web/tooling/upgrade/main.ts starts the program of HEAD on that data folder, on the port upgradeTestServer. The server finds the migrations it lacks by the set applied, makes the backup before-upgrade and runs them, or refuses to start, which fails the test.
  • What reads the same. Signed in as an administrator of the sample (and as the person with HR for the work days of everybody), the driver reads through the API the issues (the list and the count of the search), the comments and the time entries of every issue, the work days of every person, the away times of the person of the goal, the own themes and the agents, and holds each against the dump the old program wrote (web/tooling/upgrade/judge.ts, which names every count that differs and the part of an old dump that is missing). Besides the counts it holds a list of known records against the events of the dump (web/tooling/upgrade/known.ts), each found by its key: the first and the last issue whose title no other issue has, with its status; the comments of one such issue; the time entries of one such issue on one day; and one finished work day of one person, with its stretches. The run fails when the list of backups lacks the backup the upgrade made (recorded as made by the upgrade, and found in the folder), or when bugaboo security-log verify finds the log broken afterwards. The run is the acceptance test ops_06_the_sample_of_the_previous_milestone_reads_the_same_after_the_upgrade.

What a start does when a migration fails, a backup cannot be made or the database is newer is tested in the store on both databases with a migration that fails only in the tests (crates/bb-store/src/migrations/tests.rs, crates/bb-store/src/tests/upgrade.rs), and the words and exit code of the stop in the server (crates/bb-server/src/tests/upgrade.rs).

Enforced by: TEST-UPGRADE (xtask/src/checks/test_upgrade.rs: the upgrade test is there, asks Git for the tag and names none by hand, and cargo xtask ci runs it as a step that nothing switches off: alone in the list of steps or in needs_browser_app, which skips it only while web/app/package.json is missing).

Local ports (ADR-0023)

Your machine runs other Vite projects, so Bugaboo never uses default ports. All ports live in tools/dev/ports.json (single source); Vite, Playwright, the server and xtask read them from there, and every tool uses strictPort, so a busy port fails with a clear message instead of silently moving.

OffsetUsed by
0Bugaboo server in development (API + embedded app)
1Vite dev server (hot reload)
2Vite preview of a production build
3Server instance for end-to-end tests (fresh sample database)
4Vitest UI
10–29Parallel Playwright workers, one server and database each
30Load-test server
31Server of the upgrade test (cargo xtask upgrade-test)
40Throwaway PostgreSQL for tests (cargo xtask db start)

The offsets are inside a block of 100 ports. Each work folder bugaboo.winN has its own block, starting at 47200 + (N − 1) · 100 (win1 47200–47299, win3 47400–47499, up to win9 48000–48099), so folders that build and test at the same time never share a port; any other folder uses block 1 and BUGABOO_PORT_BLOCK names another one. The table above shows block 1: the server of the first folder is on 47200, of the third on 47400.

The installed product asks for its port in the setup wizard (suggesting 8443 and checking that it's free); these development ports never appear in a customer installation.

Security: threat model and personal-data flows

Part of the security and data-flow documentation (COMP-07) for the CRA technical file and for customers' own risk assessments. It covers what is built so far and grows with every milestone: each milestone review checks that new entry points appear here.

The method is STRIDE per trust boundary (boundaries from Context). Every threat names the mitigation and what proves it: a check from the catalogue (tools/checks/catalog.toml), a test, or review when a person decides.

Scope (status: M7 built, M8 planned)

In scope nowComes later (own section then)
HTTPS and start-up config, security headers, sign-in (password, passkey, two-step codes), sessions, invitations, first-run setup code, rate limits, the security log, stored secrets, logs (M1); the permission engine (roles, groups, assignments, No access, field masks, Who sees people), projects and short names, access keys, two-step sign-in by role, settings in layers (M2); issues with their text, comments, tags and labels, own fields, layouts, edit locks and drafts, changing many issues and the background jobs that carry it (M3); attachments, mail and workflows (M4); search and lists (M5); time on issues and working hours (M6); the assistant, AI apps through MCP and agents (M7)The timeline, work times and own themes (M8; threats below, planned), Remove a person and exports (M9), webhooks (M12), the served model's control plane (M14)

  ai -- "5 · HTTPS" --> provider

Entry points in M1: the HTTPS listener (pages, assets, /api/v1, /health/*), the console and bugaboo.toml, and the data folder on disk. M2 adds no new listener: the new routes are below /api/v1, and scripts reach them with an access key (Authorization: Bearer bb_…) instead of a cookie. The sample-organization program (bb-sample) is a developer tool and is not shipped before OPS-12. M7 adds no listener either: /mcp, the metadata documents and the OAuth routes are on the same port, and the server becomes a client of the AI provider (boundary 5, Server ↔ AI provider), which it calls only when an administrator switched AI on, with one exception: Try the provider may call while AI is still off. It sends only the fixed try text and no data of the organization, needs the agreement of an outside provider first, and is limited to one try in 10 seconds per person.

Issues, text and editing (M3)

M3 stores text that people write and shows it to others, and lets several people edit one issue. Each row names the test that proves it (M3 plan).

Workflows, files and notifications (M4)

M4 takes files from people, sends mail out of the server for the first time, and lets workflows decide who may change a status. Each row names the check or test that proves it; the packages add the test names (M4 plan). A test named in a cell next to a check that holds a list of required tests must be in that list. Enforced by: DOC-PROVEN-BY.

STRIDEThreatMitigationProven by

M5 lets people type searches that become database queries, search the text of issues, and share saved searches. Each row names the check that proves it; the packages add the test names (M5 plan).

Time and working hours (M6)

M6 stores what people spent their time on and when they worked (ADR-0035). Working hours are sensitive employee data (PRIV-09): the main threat is that somebody learns about another person's time without the permission for it, by any way out of the server. Each row names the check that proves it; the packages add the test names (M6 plan).

STRIDEThreatMitigationProven by

A notification about a day goes to the person of the day only; no search field, export or list reads work days (ADR-0035, decision 8)SEC-MATRIX (the routes of work days and of Working hours of others for every starting role, HR included, and with Totals only on; the notifications and e-mail channels); the tests of WP-06 and WP-10

Assistant, AI apps and agents (M7)

M7 lets AI read and change Bugaboo in three ways: the assistant (it only proposes), outside AI apps that act for a person through MCP, and agents that work on their own on what a person handed over (ADR-0013, ADR-0029, ADR-0042). The new boundary is 5, Server ↔ AI provider: text leaves the server for a provider the organization chose, and what comes back is untrusted. The main threats are that AI reads or changes more than its person, and that text in an issue steers it. The packages add the test names (M7 plan).

STRIDEThreatMitigationProven by
Elevation of privilegeAn AI app or an agent reads or changes more than its person may, or than its scope, its work or its limits allowEvery call is a tool of the one registry, run as the actor through bb-policy: a grant or key is the person narrowed by See only or See and change; an agent is its person's evaluation intersected with its work and limits, and never holds a permission of kind Manage or Take over text someone else is editing; what no key holds no grant holds. tools/list offers a tool only where the actor could use it in some project, with the permission its use case checks (Need of the registry: the constant the use case checks, NEEDED_TO_CREATE, NEEDED_TO_COMMENT or NEEDED_TO_BOOK, or the rule of bb-policy that changing an issue uses, CHANGES_ISSUES); a project kept from AI allows no tool, and only while the organization holds no project does a role for the whole organization decide (as it will in the first project), so a No access row counts as it does for the call; a call is judged by the use case at its place, so a tool left out is refused thereSEC-MATRIX (the actor kinds person via app and agent, the entry points mcp and assistant), ARCH-AI-TOOLS, ARCH-PERMS; the tests of WP-04 and WP-05, ai_04_a_tool_is_offered_only_to_a_person_who_may_use_it_somewhere, ai_04_tools_list_offers_only_the_tools_a_person_may_use_somewhere, ai_04_a_tool_allowed_only_in_projects_kept_from_ai_is_not_offered, ai_04_an_app_of_an_administrator_is_offered_the_tools_before_any_project_exists, ai_04_once_there_are_projects_they_decide_which_tools_an_app_is_offered

Timeline, work times and own themes (M8)

M8 plans with people and lets an organization or a person make a theme of their own (ADR-0030 and its amendment M8, ADR-0043, ADR-0026, update M8). It adds no listener: the style sheet of an own theme (/themes/{id}.css) and the new routes are on the same port, and the content security policy stays style-src 'self'. Work times are employee data (PRIV-09) and an away time can hint at health (GDPR Art. 9), so the main threats are that somebody learns another person's work times, and that a plan turns into a judgement of how fast a person works (COMP-10). An own theme reaches every page of the people who use it, so the other main threat is that its values carry code or make the page unreadable. The packages add the test names (M8 plan).

STRIDEThreatMitigationProven by
Information disclosureA person learns another person's away times, usual work days, work hours, shares or choice of Holidays through the timeline, Group by person, a warning, the card of a bar, a notification, a search, an export or an AI tool (PRIV-09, PRIV-12)Work times are the kind of people information Work times (Who sees people): others see an away time only as Away, never its note, and a reader who does not see the person on a bar gets no Away, only the neutral warning Days without work, which comes alike for absences, holidays and days off. No search field and no export of M8 reads work times, the tool registry has no tool that reads them, and a notification about them goes to their person onlySEC-MATRIX (the routes of work times and the timeline, for every starting role and each choice of Work times), ARCH-PERSON-REF, ARCH-AI-TOOLS; the tests of WP-04, WP-06 and WP-10

Information disclosureThe time factor becomes a score of a person: listed, sorted, grouped or totalled across issues, kept per person, or set or proposed by AI (PRIV-09, COMP-10)It belongs to the issue and goes back to ×1 when the first assigned person changes; the search language has no word for it, no list offers it as a column and no total uses it; no tool of the registry changes it (ADR-0030, amendment M8)ARCH-AI-TOOLS, SEC-MATRIX; the tests of WP-06
TamperingA person enters or changes another person's work times without Enter work times for others, or sets a share in a project without Decide who has which role thereThe use case judges the permission before every change of another person's work times or a share; the routes declare it; no key and no agent holds Enter work times for others (ADR-0025, amendment M8)ARCH-PERMS, SEC-MATRIX; the tests of WP-04

Elevation of privilege, information disclosureA person makes or changes a theme for everyone without the right, or reads somebody else's personal theme or draftThemes for everyone need Change organization settings; a personal theme is served to its maker only, and any other request gets the answer of a theme that does not existSEC-MATRIX (the routes of themes and their style sheets); the tests of WP-05
Denial of serviceA theme for everyone makes the page unreadable, or a broken theme leaves people with no usable lookA theme for everyone with a pair that is Hard to read is refused; a choice that names an own theme that is gone counts as the built-in theme it extended (ADR-0026, update M8)STY-CONTRAST; the tests of WP-05 and WP-08
Denial of serviceA large timeline, a flood of moves or a huge upload of a theme slows the server for everyoneThe timeline answers a page of rows within the budget of timeline data (PERF-01); the number of own themes and the size of an upload are named limits, and changes count against the rate limits of a personPERF-BENCH (the timeline of the biggest project on 1 M issues), PERF-N1; the tests of WP-05 and WP-12

The command reads the whole log every time; the status page reads only the entries added since its last good check (and the whole log again once a day), and keeps its answer for a few seconds unless the server wrote an entry in between, so a long log does not make every visit slow (M1-F60)hash-chain property tests sec_15_any_changed_row_breaks_the_chain and sec_15_a_rewritten_tail_without_the_key_does_not_verify; security-log tests (WP-05); ops_08_the_status_page_checks_only_new_entries_and_the_command_checks_all (bb-store), ops_08_the_status_page_follows_the_log_and_reuses_its_answer_until_something_is_written

Accepted risks

RiskWhy acceptedRevisit
Somebody whom a share reaches and who holds the ID of a saved search can tell, by the time an answer takes or by a page of Shared with me that ends at the bound of names (a short page with the last search shown as its cursor, then an empty page), that a search shared with them exists and passes the check of its fields but fails on a name they cannot know (a person they are not shown by name, a group they are not in, an issue they do not read): resolving that name reads from the store, and a search that does not exist, does not reach them or fails an earlier check does notEvery one of these is the same answer: the status, the code and the body of not found. A search that does not exist, one that does not reach the person and one that fails the check of its fields run the same reads. The ID is random (80 bits) and is only known from a link or an event. What leaks is that a search that the person who shared it chose to share with them exists and fails on some name, never which name, and the receiver cannot choose the text (ADR-0034, decision 4 and item 8)sec_06_a_hidden_saved_search_and_a_missing_one_run_the_same_reads (the same reads), qry_06_a_search_that_does_not_check_for_the_receiver_is_not_there_for_any_call (the same answers); revisit when a search can be shared outside the organization
The preview of a file that is stored already shows as soon as the job of its attachment runs, while the preview of a new file is made first and takes longer, so somebody who watches when a preview appears can tell, a little, that the same content was stored beforeThe statuses and links in every answer are the same; the person already holds the content; a delay as long as the slowest preview would make every picture wait, so none is added (ADR-0032 §4)When files get rules of their own (M9, GDPR handling of file bytes)
Finishing a file that is stored already is a little faster than finishing a new one, so somebody who measures the time can tell that the same content was stored beforeThe answers are the same (no preview, no link, no status of the other attachment); the person already holds the content; equal time would mean reading and writing the file again for nothing (ADR-0032)When files get rules of their own (M9, GDPR handling of file bytes)
On Windows the child of a preview has a limit on its heap and none on its address spaceNo safe crate sets the memory limit of a job object and unsafe code is forbidden; the child is pure Rust and the allocator refuses what would pass 1 GiB (ADR-0032)When a safe way to set the limit exists
An administrator of the host machine can read the master keyAnyone with full control of the host can read process memory too; protection against them is out of scope for self-hosted installationsM14 (served model: keys per customer, operator without data access)
Somebody who controls the host (and so reads keys/log.key and can rewrite logs/security-head.log) can forge the security logThe log protects against attackers who reach only the database; the same control lets them read process memory and the master keyM14 (served model: keys per customer, operator without data access)
Somebody who keeps failing at an account can make it wait, up to 15 minutes at a time once the windows have grown (the limit counts failures and a success clears them, so it is never a lock for good)Any limit that stops guessing can be used to slow the person down; a permanent lock would be worse (SEC-14)When the settings registry takes the numbers (OPS-10)
A security-log entry that cannot be written (the anchor file or the database fails) is reported in the server log but does not undo or refuse the sign-in. The server counts the entries it could not write since it started, and the status page warns when the count is above zero (sec_15_the_status_page_warns_when_a_log_entry_could_not_be_written); the status page and bugaboo security-log verify also name a database that lacks the newest entries that the anchor file knows of (a restore from an older backup, lost writes or a cut-off end) and say what to check (sec_15_the_status_page_warns_when_the_anchor_is_ahead)A sign-in that fails because the log is full would let anybody who can fill the disk lock everybody outThe decision stays (M1-F40, done in M2 WP-04)
Check access tells a checker that a role comes from a project you can't see, so they learn that such a project exists above, never its name or anything in itA sentence that leaves the row out would explain a decision wrongly; only people who can check access at that place see it (ADR-0025, decision 12)When restricted projects need more (SEC-05, V1)
The version of a move preview is a digest of the tree, who has which role and the levels the roles set, so somebody who keeps asking for the preview of a project they see can tell that something changed in a project they cannot seeThe preview is what Show, then do needs and a stale one is refused; the digest is opaque and names nothing, no count and no place, and the person only learns that the preview is old (ADR-0025, decision 12)When restricted projects need more (SEC-05, V1)
A person who holds both Manage roles and Decide who has which role for the whole organization can give themselves HR and so read and change everybody's working hoursNobody holds the two permissions at the start, so without the exception nobody could give HR; an administrator holds every other permission and so can give every other role already. The gift is in the security log, and the people whose hours are read are not told of each reading (ADR-0025, amendment M6)When the security log can tell named people of such a gift (M9)
People with Decide who has which role from above keep it on a project where they have No access, and see its name and short name thereOtherwise a project lead could shut the administrators out for good (ADR-0025, decision 6)—
The child that makes a preview holds the rights of the server account: protection is the separation of the process and the limits on memory, time and pixels, not a sandbox. A memory-safety bug in image, hayro or vello_cpu (they use unsafe inside, though our code does not) lets a crafted file run code in the child, which can then read the keys and the database of the server account and reach the networkThe libraries are pure Rust with only the gif, jpeg, png and webp decoders compiled in, and the child reads its input from standard input with limits; a sandbox needs system calls that code without unsafe cannot make today. The row of denial of service above says what the limits stop (crashes and bombs), not a compromise. On a small host, five previews at once may use 5 GiB of heapM4-F121 (landlock or seccomp on Linux, a separate user, a restricted token on Windows once a safe crate exists)
A person who may change their handle can learn once for each change whether one handle is taken (name.taken, or the handle of a group or a role), because a free handle is changed at once and starts the 7-day clock; a few refused tries are allowed firstHandles are made from names, so a guess is cheap, but the limits leave a person at most 20 answers taken in a day (TAKEN_ANSWERS_PER_DAY, counted per person, reserved in one step so parallel tries cannot pass the last one, after which every handle gets the same try again later) and, for each change, one more. The day is a fixed window from the first answer counted, so a person can get up to about 40 across the turn of a day; each server process counts for itself and a restart forgets the count, so with several processes the bound is 20 a day for each process; the refused tries of a minute only pace it. A person who never changed their handle has no 7-day clock, so the bound is 20 a day without end, for each account; the handle is shown wherever a mention is, and a mention follows Who sees peopleWhen a handle is judged apart from the rest of the person's data
While the list of domains for signing up is empty (open sign-up), a few networks can use up the cap on sign-up e-mails (ADDRESSES_PER_HOUR_MAX = 100 addresses an hour for the whole server): each network may make SIGN_UP_REQUESTS_PER_HOUR = 20 requests an hour, so five networks fill the cap, and real sign-up e-mails are then dropped without a word until the hour is overThe cap keeps strangers from receiving mail in bulk, and the server has to be cheaper to fill than to keep silent: the cap is the safer failure. The answer stays the same for every address; for sign-ups the cap counts only while anybody may sign up, so a list of approved domains (the first thing to set) takes the cap away for them; the links to a new e-mail address (PRIV-06) share the memory and the cap and always count, because a new address can be anywhere; the moment the cap is reached is written once to the security log (sign_up.mail_capped); the request limit per network is held well under the cap by a const assertM4-F128 (review: a decision of the lead, a note for administrators when sign-up e-mails were capped, M9)
A plus tag (a+1@b.co) is another address to Bugaboo and often the same mailbox for the mail server, so one mailbox can be signed up several timesThe limit is 5 sign-up tries a minute for a network and the cap of the server; stripping tags would change addresses that are realWhen signing up is next changed
Whoever holds Change organization settings (or a stolen administrator session) can point mail.host and mail.port at the internal network and tell open ports apart from the answers of the test e-mailOne try in 10 seconds; changing the host deletes the stored password; the right is the one that sets the whole server upM4-F123 (ask for the password again before mail.* changes)
A Guest can mention a role and so e-mail everyone who holds itAt most 50 mentions in a text and one e-mail in 5 minutes for each issue; the mention follows the writer's rights and the recipient has to see the issueM4-F124 (review: a decision of the lead on mentions)
The editor of a workflow lists the names of all roles to a person who manages workflows, while the list of roles needs Manage roles or Decide who has which roleThe names are needed to choose Who can do it; it matters only for custom rolesM4-F125
An AI app that holds an access key of a person reads, through /api/v1, a field or a project that is Never sent to AIThe mark keeps text away from AI that Bugaboo calls and from the tools of the registry (/mcp included); a key is the person's own way in for scripts, and Bugaboo cannot tell a script from an app. The key reads only what its person may read, narrowed by its choice (ADR-0025, decision 8), and the person chose to give it to the appWhen AI-24 (M12) shows the use of each app, or when keys can be limited to /mcp
Self-signed certificates show a browser warningSafer than plain HTTP; admins can provide a certificate, ACME comes in 1.0V1 (ACME)
A request with an access key takes a little different time depending on what is wrong with the key (not shaped like a key, unknown, ran out): only somebody who holds a whole secret can tell that it ran out, and the answer is the sameEqual time needs a dummy lookup and protects nothing against a person who already holds the secretM2-F51: when a measurement shows a difference that does not need a secret

No personal data leaves the server in M1: no mail, no AI, no outside fonts, scripts or analytics (PRIV-01).

Personal data in M2

M2 adds where people work (groups and roles), projects, access keys and each person's own settings. The marks below are decided here (ADR-0025); each package writes them on its entities, and cargo xtask gen privacy then lists them on the generated page docs/privacy/personal-data.md. Enforced by: DATA-MARKS.

A new category, organization: where a person works, meaning their groups and the roles they have, and where. Its legal basis is the contract (Art. 6(1)(b); for employees in Germany together with Art. 88 GDPR and § 26 BDSG): an organization cannot give people work in projects without recording who may do what.

flowchart LR
  admin(["Administrator or project lead"])
  person(["Person"])
  script(["Script or app<br/>with an access key"])
  subgraph bb["Bugaboo"]
    groups["Groups and members"]
    assign["Who has which role<br/>person or group, role or No access, project"]
    rules["Field levels and Who sees people<br/>(no personal data)"]
    keys["Access keys<br/>owner, name, hashed secret,<br/>last use (to the minute)"]
    mine["My settings<br/>time zone, region, appearance, shortcuts"]
    policy["bb-policy<br/>evaluation per request"]
    seclog["Security log"]
  end
  admin -- "manages" --> groups & assign & rules
  person -- "chooses" --> mine
  person -- "makes" --> keys
  script -- "Bearer key" --> keys --> policy
  groups & assign & rules --> policy

Personal data in M4

M3 added the text of people (issues, comments, own fields) and M4 adds files, mail and notifications. M4 is the first time data leaves the server: an e-mail carries the address of the person and, unless the person or the organization chose Short e-mails, the title of an issue, the text of a comment and the names of people to the mail server that an administrator entered. Nothing else leaves: no AI, no outside fonts, scripts or analytics (PRIV-01). The marks of every field are on the generated page docs/privacy/personal-data.md; the flows and the times are here (COMP-07).

Storage limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(e)) is the organization's judgement: Bugaboo deletes no working hours by itself, shows how many are past the keep period, and makes deleting them one step (ADR-0035, decision 7).

Personal data in M8

M8 stores when and how much people work, so that the timeline can plan with them, and a time factor on issues (ADR-0030 and its amendment M8). Nothing about work times leaves the server, except the e-mail of a notification to the person themselves when they switch it on (ADR-0033, amendment M8). No access key reads them: the routes of work times take a session only, and the timeline answers a key with nobody's work times (no hatched day, no Away, no Too much at once) and with the bars of the dates people set, not planned by effort.

What a bar may tell of another person's work times. A reader whose Who sees people level for Work times is Hidden still gets bars planned by effort and the warning Not enough days, because the plan needs them (the maintainer's decision, M8 review). The length of such a bar can tell how many days the person works in the project; it never tells which days are away, which are holidays or days off, or why: those days are hatched and named only to a reader who may know the person's work times, and Away and Too much at once go only to that reader. The card of a bar follows the same line (M8, the card of a bar): its effort and the number of work days it takes go to every reader who may read Estimated time (the work days only when the bars are planned by effort, so never to an access key), while the person's usual work days, their work hours and their share in the project go only to a reader who may know the person's work times, may read Assigned to and sees the person by name (a weekday without work would else read as an absence; plan_12_the_card_of_a_bar_tells_effort_and_work_time_only_as_far_as_allowed). The effort divided by its work days gives the average minutes a day the person can give the issue, which is what the length of the bar tells such a reader already. A reader who may not read Assigned to gets no hatched day and no warning about the person on the bar, so neither the list nor its count tells that the issue has one; a reader who sees the person by role only or under Hidden gets every day without work as one neutral kind (no-work): away, holiday and day off look and read the same, with no word, so nobody learns that a day was an absence (the maintainer's decision of 2026-11-13; plan_11_a_reader_who_does_not_see_the_person_sees_every_day_without_work_alike), and instead of Away that reader gets the neutral warning Days without work over the days of the bar, which comes alike for an away day, a holiday or a day off on a weekday of the bar and has no way out but Keep and accept, because Move it after and Make it longer would tell the away days (plan_13_a_reader_who_does_not_see_the_person_gets_only_days_without_work, plan_13_days_without_work_fire_for_a_holiday_as_for_an_away_day; the maintainer's decision of 2026-11-13). Too much at once about such a person is not listed. Keep and accept follows the same rule: a kind not told to the person who accepts is refused like a kind the issue does not have, so accepting is never a test for an absence (plan_13_accepting_a_kind_not_told_tests_for_no_absence). The other ways out take no kind and answer nothing about the days of a person: the preview of Move it after walks dependencies and bars, Make it longer saves a due date the person typed or confirmed, and Give it to someone else… changes Assigned to. By role only or under Hidden the days without work still carry their dates in the answer, all of one neutral kind (UX §4.7, People on the bars), so their dates are not secret from the response, while which of them were absences is. Under Group by person each person's row hatches their away days and holidays across the span, only for a reader who sees people by name and may know that person's work times (plan_10_the_row_of_a_person_hatches_their_days_as_far_as_work_times_allow). Enforced by: review (who may know which work times is decided in ADR-0030 and its amendment M8), backed by the tests named here.

What Remove a person does with the plan's records (M9, M8-F30): the time factors the person set or that are theirs as the person on the bar stay with their issues, with the person shown as Former user … like every other reference; the place in Assigned to goes with the assignment; the accepted warnings they accepted stay with their issues, accepted by Former user …. None of them is work times, so the deletion of work times does not touch them. No outside service and no AI reads work times (COMP-10), and the public holidays are computed in Bugaboo, so no service learns which state a person works in.

In Germany a works council has a say in tools that can watch how employees work (Works Constitution Act, §87 (1) no. 6). The limits of ADR-0030 (no reason stored, no factor per person, no reports) are what an organization shows its works council; Bugaboo does not decide for it.

Decision records

Each record explains one decision: the situation, what we decided, what follows from it, what else we considered, and which checks enforce it. The records are on their own page, Decision records.

  • ADR-0001: Modular monolith in one binary (Accepted)
  • ADR-0002: HTTP stack: Tokio, axum, rustls (Accepted)
  • ADR-0003: Databases: SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional (Accepted)
  • ADR-0004: Authorization: one policy engine and Authorized<T> (Accepted)
  • ADR-0005: Search language: one Rust crate, also in the browser (Accepted)
  • ADR-0006: Own fields stored in a typed value table (Accepted)
  • ADR-0007: Event log and outbox as the single source of change (Accepted)
  • ADR-0008: API first: OpenAPI from Rust, TypeScript client generated (Accepted)
  • ADR-0009: Browser app: React 19, Vite, TanStack, React Aria (Accepted)
  • ADR-0010: Styling through design tokens only (Accepted)
  • ADR-0011: One Markdown renderer for server and browser (Accepted)
  • ADR-0012: One binary for sold and served (Accepted)
  • ADR-0013: AI: one provider interface, one tool registry, no decisions about people (Accepted)
  • ADR-0014: One check runner for hooks, agents and CI (Accepted)
  • ADR-0015: Personal-data marks drive GDPR features (Accepted)
  • ADR-0016: Full-text search inside the database (Accepted)
  • ADR-0017: Background jobs stored in the database (Accepted)
  • ADR-0018: One settings registry drives storage, API and dialogs (Accepted)
  • ADR-0019: Edit locks and confirmed saves (Accepted)
  • ADR-0020: Architecture is checked by many small checks, and the checks are checked (Accepted)
  • ADR-0021: Issue IDs, counting or random (Accepted)
  • ADR-0022: Who sees people is part of the permission model (Accepted)
  • ADR-0023: Development ports and test setup (Accepted)
  • ADR-0024: Master repository in a synced folder, work folders outside it (Accepted)
  • ADR-0025: Roles, groups and assignments on the project tree (Accepted)
  • ADR-0026: One theme file for everything about how the app looks (Accepted)
  • ADR-0027: Layouts, rules per issue type and the starting workflow (Accepted)
  • ADR-0028: The message catalog is split into parts; the first page loads one (Accepted)
  • ADR-0029: AI agents: apps that act for a person, and agents that work on their own (Accepted)
  • ADR-0030: Planning with people: who works on a bar, work times, time factors and plan warnings (Accepted)
  • ADR-0031: Workflows: statuses as data, one judge for a status change (Accepted)
  • ADR-0032: Files: stored by content, checked from their content, previews in a separate process (Accepted)
  • ADR-0033: Notifications and e-mail: an outbox reader that checks again before it tells anyone (Accepted)
  • ADR-0034: Saved searches: owned by one person, shared without giving anyone more (Accepted)
  • ADR-0035: Time on issues and working hours (Accepted)
  • ADR-0036: License: AGPL-3.0-or-later, other terms from the maintainer, a contributor agreement (Accepted)
  • ADR-0037: No hosted CI; verification is local (Accepted)
  • ADR-0038: Public identity and plain commit messages (Accepted)
  • ADR-0039: Explicit master configuration; only the master publishes (Accepted)
  • ADR-0040: Version numbers follow the plan (Accepted)
  • ADR-0041: Branches are rebased, never merged (Accepted)
  • ADR-0042: The MCP server and how AI apps sign in (Accepted)
  • ADR-0043: Dates and dependencies (Accepted)
  • ADR-0044: Download my data and Remove a person (Accepted)
  • ADR-0045: Keep and delete rules (Accepted)
  • ADR-0046: Backups, restore and upgrades (Accepted)
  • ADR-0047: Releases: signatures, the parts list, the support period and vulnerability handling (Accepted)
  • ADR-0048: Support access with the customer's approval (Accepted)
